## The form that refuses completion

Against the black field of *Ex Nihilo (Cosmos) #248*, segmented white traces gather, fracture, and scatter. Some runs suggest polygonal edges; others break before contour can form. Slanting lines briefly imply a dodecahedron, then disperse into particulate atmosphere. The eye labors to assemble a solid.

Reas's Still Life series subjects the five Platonic solids to pixels, color channels, shaders, display buffers, screens, and time. Mathematical form appears through a sequence of material and technical decisions. Calculation supplies structure; performance determines appearance.

*Ex Nihilo (Cosmos)* sharpens this proposition through continuous change. Traditional still life offers objects arranged for prolonged inspection. Reas retains that concentrated attention to relation, surface, balance, and objecthood while setting every composition in motion. The dodecahedron persists as a possibility carried by operations that continually rearrange it.

## From geometry to a live picture

The Still Life series began with *There’s No Distance* at bitforms in 2016. The exhibition framed Reas’s software works as performances rather than images made once in a studio and subsequently delivered to a gallery. As Reas put it in the exhibition material, there is no distance between an audience and the image being made: each encounter is an unrepeatable event.[^1] The new Still Life works were described as simulated compositions that deconstruct Platonic solids and flatten their planes into a single visual field. Their subject was pure geometry rather than the natural world.

The phrase “pure geometry” needs care. It can make the series sound like an escape from history or matter. Reas’s method keeps those conditions in view. A cube, tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron, or icosahedron is an ideal object only in abstraction. In a software environment it must be modeled, sampled, colored, rasterized, and presented. When multiple planes appear at once, the solid no longer guarantees ordinary perspective. The image becomes a negotiation between measurable structure and the viewer’s unstable reconstruction of it.

The 2023–24 bitforms exhibition *It Doesn’t Exist (In Any Other Form)* shows the scale of that negotiation. The show described Still Life as conceptual software painting through simulation and computer graphics, and placed long-form generative works beside video, plotter drawings, woodblock prints, and blockchain-based pieces.[^2] Reas tests the same pictorial problem across supports while keeping the manifestations distinct. A plotter drawing can make a line’s discreteness and color separation palpable; a print can hold a state for prolonged looking; a screen or projection can reveal the temporal behavior that a print must arrest.

Meredith Hoy’s “Painting as Programming” gives this double commitment a precise critical account. Hoy argues that Reas’s work holds conceptual procedure and painterly surface together. It turns the executable nature of code into a condition of visual richness, refusing the premise that software art must resolve into a transparent diagram or a decorative skin.[^3] Still Life brings that proposition to a point of strain. The more vividly a solid appears, the more insistently the work exposes the operations—pixels, lines, changing channels, moving layers—through which it appears. The picture’s seduction becomes inseparable from its refusal to be stable.

## Plato after rasterization

The official description of *Ex Nihilo (Cosmos)* makes Plato’s Theory of Forms the project’s explicit conceptual backdrop. It identifies the dodecahedron as Cosmos within the five-solid sequence—Cube/Earth, Tetrahedron/Fire, Octahedron/Air, Dodecahedron/Cosmos, Icosahedron/Water—and describes the work as the generation of images from code rather than physical material.[^4] The account is historically pointed; it does not establish that Reas retrieves a timeless philosophy untouched by media. The work’s dodecahedron is an effect generated in the image by operations that construct and disturb it.

*Ex Nihilo* carries geometry through incompatible representational systems. The project description says pixels are translated into lines of varying position and color, producing fields that oscillate between structure and dissolution.[^5] The verb “translated” is important: model, pixel value, line, screen, and visual inference each produce loss and possibility. The viewer encounters the difficulty of holding an ideal form through changing material signs.

Platonic solids matter because their regularity supplies a rigorous test for Reas's visual system. They are useful precisely because one believes one knows what they should be. The work activates that expectation, then prevents the form from settling. In the Still Life series, Reas also inherits the problems of modern abstraction: how can an image organize a field without representing an object in ordinary space? His contribution is to make the underlying operation executable and temporal. A line is generated rather than simply placed; its relation to another line may change before the viewer has finished reading it.

Nora N. Khan’s phrase “disconcerting software paintings,” written of Reas’s 2016 work, remains useful as critical pressure.[^6] The disturbance is not technological novelty alone. The Still Lifes give viewers enough formal coherence to invite comparison with painting—balance, mass, chromatic counterpoint, layered depth—then make that coherence unstable. They require a viewer to remain with an object that is becoming different while it is being seen.

## #248: white lines, black ground, delayed cosmos

The Museum’s #248 makes this visual problem severe. Granular white lines cut across a deep black ground. Some clusters are short and nearly horizontal; others rise diagonally or curve into broken arcs. Their segmentation makes them appear drawn and digital at once: marks made with a dry instrument and sampled data refusing continuous contour.[^7]

The black ground does more than provide contrast. It makes every white segment read as a decision in an otherwise unbounded space. At times, several segments align strongly enough to imply an edge of a solid. At other times, a disrupted line prevents the implication from becoming an object. The dodecahedron is continually proposed by the field and continually interrupted by it.

Object #248 produces a distinctive rhythm of looking. A conventional perspective image permits the eye to establish a framework and then move within it. #248 reverses that sequence. The eye searches for a framework, finds a provisional one, and is sent back to the local behavior of lines. The relation between near and far also remains unstable. White clusters sometimes float forward like bright dust; sometimes they seem to form a deep scaffold receding into the black. The image makes depth an optical event rather than a settled spatial fact.

The live work heightens the effect. The official project account describes a continuously running, non-repeating system and assigns controls for channels, white state, speed, pause, and a new Still Life state.[^8] The Museum records a small mismatch between published controls and the reviewed generator, so display instructions must distinguish the project’s published interface from the current observed implementation.[^9] A visitor encounters the work through that interface, with its specific conditions, rather than through a frictionless route to an abstract form.

The spacebar’s “new Still Life” names a field of behavior in which a viewer can provoke a new state. The Museum record does not establish that this state is determined solely by the original token parameters, so it is described here as a viewer-triggered manifestation rather than a canonical token image.[^10] The action clarifies the work’s wager: a geometrical form enters the work through time, variation, and user encounter. Cosmos arrives as an event that can begin again.

## Color systems, supports, and the problem of the “still”

The Still Life series treats color as structure rather than expressive finish. bitforms describes RGB and HSB variants as alternative technical color spaces and shows how printed, plotter, and long-form works make their differences visible.[^11] RGB names an additive screen logic; HSB organizes hue, saturation, and brightness in a manner often closer to perceptual adjustment. Reas relocates painting’s color problems into systems where a palette can be parameterized, separated into channels, toggled, recomputed, and distributed across a field that changes in time.

Display is part of the medium. A screen-based Still Life is no more a neutral delivery device than a canvas is a neutral support. Screen size, orientation, black level, projector light, frame rate, browser, and duration alter what the viewer sees. The 2023 bitforms record for *Still Life (HSB D)* specifies custom software, computer, screen or projector, variable dimensions, and portrait or landscape orientation.[^12] The work is a set of relations that must be staged, not an image file scaled up or down at will.

For *Ex Nihilo*, the point is even sharper because the dodecahedral suggestion depends on a black field, white segmentation, and changing depth. A bright gallery with an inadequate display could flatten the interval between line and ground on which the work depends. A still screenshot can preserve one compositional state, but it cannot establish duration, responsiveness, or later variations. The Museum’s accession-era captures are time-specific documentation surrogates; their original visual bytes were not retained, and any later preservation capture must be identified as later.[^13]

The preservation limit is central to the series’s aesthetics. Reas calls these works still lifes while making persistence impossible. A display should let viewers understand that each visible formation is both a picture and an instance of a process. The series’s proximity to painting lies in its demand for prolonged looking rather than a promise of a final image.

## Pause, restart, and the ethics of a state

The controls make a second kind of “stillness” possible: a temporary decision to stop. The published project account assigns `P` to pause, while the spacebar produces a new Still Life state.[^8] This pair gives duration a visible structure. To pause is to turn a passing configuration into an occasion for looking; to restart is to acknowledge that this configuration has no exclusive claim to the work. The viewer can inhabit a state without mistaking it for an original that the software has finally delivered.

That relation complicates the curator’s usual task of choosing an image. A museum will often need a poster image, accessibility description, documentation capture, or orienting moment for a gallery visitor. Such selections help viewers look; they cannot confer priority on a single frame. #248 has an exact token-bound identity, while its visible states remain time-specific manifestations. The Museum distinguishes those states from accession-era documentation rather than treating a surrogate as a canonical image.[^10][^13]

A viewer may pause, change the state, or use documented display controls, while the range of possible appearances remains authored and technically bounded. The recorded control mismatch makes the work’s dependence on interface legible: an ideal form is encountered through specifications, runtime, and a present display situation.[^9] This is a concrete display condition.

For #248, pause is a curatorial verb. It asks the viewer to sustain attention to a configuration long enough for the broken white lines to suggest a cosmos, then releases that suggestion back into the work’s continuous becoming. The still life is the practice of looking carefully while knowing that the form will not hold.

## Reception and counter-pressure

Reas’s institutions and platforms have often presented this work through the language of innovation, simulation, and the expanded field of digital art. That history is real: *There’s No Distance* placed early and later work in relation, bitforms’ 2023 exhibition assembled screen works with prints and plotter drawings, and Art Blocks and Feral File co-presented *Ex Nihilo* in 2026.[^14] Institutional recognition can nevertheless make the series easier to admire than to see. The rhetoric of a work that “never repeats” risks becoming a generic guarantee of inexhaustibility.

The more useful response is ambivalent. Continuous change can fatigue attention; a field of many possible configurations can replace compositional decision with a spectacle of permanent becoming. The Still Life series answers that danger when its forms remain specific enough to create resistance. In #248, the black ground and segmented white marks prevent the work from becoming decorative flow. The dodecahedron remains a demanding proposition. It asks the viewer to hold a mathematical object in mind while accepting that the work will not allow the object to appear whole.

This tension also guards against a false opposition between a “pure” ideal and technical accident. The documented R/B discrepancy is a real condition of the current generator, not an allegory of human fallibility. It reminds us that no live software work is a frictionless conduit for an abstract plan. Dependencies, interfaces, and display instructions are part of the form in which the work appears. The Museum must disclose that fact without reducing the artwork to a bug report.

## The Museum object

*Ex Nihilo (Cosmos)* #248 gives accession `6529NM.2026.001` its contemporary horizon. It does not conclude Reas’s practice or turn the seven works into a retrospective. It brings several of their problems into concentrated contact: code as performance, a rule becoming image, a screen as a stage for drawing, and a static document’s inability to contain a live system. In the Museum group, CENTURY makes abstraction recombine; *Pre-Process* makes elements collide and seek equilibrium; *Phototaxis* turns behavior into trace; *923 EMPTY ROOMS* turns units into distributed space. #248 makes an ideal form appear by giving it over to temporal instability.

The work belongs in a public collection because it makes a demanding claim about digital art without confusing technology with novelty. Its Cosmos is not a system’s grand total. It is the unsteady moment in which a viewer sees a solid almost arrive, then watches it return to lines. The image has no other form because its form is the ongoing work of coming into view.

### Publication-safe summary

Punk6529 gave the 6529 Network Museum seven already-minted Art Blocks works by Casey Reas. The Museum accepted the full gift on 1 August 2026 and accessioned the seven works into the permanent collection on 2 August 2026. The Museum owns the tokens and the donor's transferable interest in them; copyright remains separate. The retained metadata identifies CC BY-NC 4.0, and the accession carries active software-preservation obligations.

### Claims not supported by the record

- that Casey Reas selected or endorsed the seven-work group;
- that the donor described a personal selection thesis or motive beyond making the full gift;
- that the three CENTURY works form an artist-designated triptych or suite;
- that the group is a retrospective, complete survey, or canonical selection;
- that token title includes copyright;
- that accession completed autonomous preservation;
- that any work was donated because of rarity, market value, or investment potential;
- that a static Art Blocks image is the complete artwork.

### Retention boundary

The initial official static PNG responses and two full-viewport screenshots for each object were referenced and hash-recorded as time-specific documentation surrogates. Their bytes were not retained in the initial public package. The [visual-observation record](../../../../records/accessions/6529NM.2026.001/visual-observation-record.json) leaves a new, attributed preservation recapture open; that future capture must be retained as a separately dated object and must not be represented as the original observation bytes. A platform thumbnail is a platform-authorized documentation state. It is never a Museum-declared canonical state unless a controlling artist, contract, or accession record explicitly gives it that status. For *Phototaxis*, the precise supported term is **the official 1,000-iteration thumbnail state**.

## 5. Shared 2026-08-02 close-looking baseline

These observations were made from the exact official token stills at original resolution. They are a common baseline, not language to copy unchanged into every essay.

| Object | Formal baseline | Questions for the object writer |
|---|---|---|
| CENTURY #31 | Circular field dominated by slate, saturated blue, and cream. Dense vertical slices interrupt diagonal cream and pale-salmon lines. Large curved cream forms are partly buried by the slicing structure. | How do the near-central splices change scale and continuity? Does the tondo-like boundary stabilize or intensify the fractured interior? What changes after interactive recomposition? |
| CENTURY #724 | Broad cream field with rust-red arcs and upper bands. Sparse charcoal and salmon diagonals cross large negative areas; a dark lower-right crescent and isolated lower verticals hold the open field. | How does openness alter the project's characteristic density? Does the work feel suspended, cut apart, or unfinished in a productive sense? How does Janky manifest without using the label as explanation? |
| CENTURY #401 | Gray field, black vertical columns, white diagonals, and translucent circular or arc forms. Slices read as both surface interruption and shallow architectural depth. | How do opacity and grayscale change the relation between slicing and motion? Which planes appear in front, and why does depth remain unstable? |
| Pre-Process #63 | Panoramic black-and-white composition in three horizontal registers. Dark circular masses attach to axial bands while repeated translucent arcs record movement, collision, and accumulation. | How does the 1.78 ratio make this different from a square field? How do the repeated axes discipline the apparent turbulence? What does the official static output disclose, and what changes during execution? |
| Phototaxis #308 | Pale cyan and gray trajectories produce an outer elliptical circulation around a dense lower-central knot, with a second convergence above and long escaping paths. | How does the official 1,000-iteration thumbnail state convert duration into density, curvature, and reach? How do three light positions organize the image without being visible? What changes as execution continues? |
| 923 EMPTY ROOMS #713 | Acid-green diagonal raster crosses a charcoal field but breaks around voids that imply a cornered room. A luminous right seam and bright lower ledge produce simultaneous recession and optical vibration. | Which elements correspond to the exact `555536` colorform sequence? How does the room emerge from absence rather than outline? What does the diagram toggle reveal? |
| Ex Nihilo (Cosmos) #248 | Segmented white traces cross black in unstable polygonal and dodecahedral suggestions. Interruption and scale change create layered depth without a settled solid. | How does a continuous non-repeating display change the meaning of this still? How do channel, speed, pause, and regeneration controls affect the encounter? How should the documented R/B control discrepancy be presented? |

## 9. Conflicts, naming problems, and do-not-collapse rules

### 9.1 Phototaxis date

Art Blocks and the 2021 artist technical note support a 2021 release. The current artist NFT register lists 2022. Use “developed/released for Art Blocks in 2021” where discussing documented activity, and note the current artist-register discrepancy. Do not silently normalize all dates to 2022.

### 9.2 923 versus 924

The retained project population contains 924 invocations numbered 0-923. Invocation 0 is separately coded `999999`; invocations 1-923 form the documented combinatorial sequence. The project title and artistic combinatorics refer to 923 rooms; the release population is 924. State both at the appropriate level. Do not invent an artistic theory for invocation 0.

### 9.3 Still Life dates

The current artist Atomism page describes Still Life software as 2015-2023; the 2016 bitforms exhibition anchors the public debut of the early works. Write “developed from 2015 and publicly presented in 2016” unless a more exact object history is established.

### 9.4 There's No Distance

The title names both the 2016 bitforms exhibition and a 2023 black-and-white long-form work extending Still Life. Always specify exhibition or project and date. Do not collapse them.

### 9.5 CENTURY dates

The wider CENTURY body begins in 2012. The donated tokens belong to the 2021 Art Blocks project. Use both dates and state what each one dates.

### 9.6 Pre-Process dates

The system originates in 2003, appeared in unresolved form in 2005, and was completed/released as a 120-work Art Blocks project in 2022. Do not date the tokenized work simply “2003,” and do not erase its archaeology by calling it only a 2022 project.

### 9.7 Artist name typography

Machine records use Casey REAS. The artist's current site often uses REAS. Normal editorial prose may use Casey Reas. Preserve exact capitalization in formal record quotations and titles.

### 9.8 Feral File founding

Use the institution's own account: Feral File grew from the 2019 a2p exchange and was co-founded in 2020 by Casey Reas and Sean Moss-Pultz in the Bitmark context. Avoid flattening organization/company/person roles if a sentence requires legal precision.

### 9.9 Token, artwork, image, code

- The token records chain identity, edition, and transfer history; title, copyright, accession, and interpretation are recorded separately.
- The script and token hash are constitutive inputs for these Art Blocks works.
- The generator executes the work in a browser/runtime environment.
- The static PNG is a project-authorized or platform-generated documentation state, not the whole live work.
- A Museum screenshot or video is documentation unless an artist-approved manifestation says otherwise.

The controlling presenter record is [Bright Moments, “923 EMPTY ROOMS”](https://www.brightmoments.io/923emptyrooms). Use this exact six-city schedule and mapping:

## 10. Critical argument bank

These are propositions to test, not conclusions to repeat automatically.

1. Reas's enduring subject is the interval between instruction and event.
2. The visible image is often a history of relations rather than a picture of an object.
3. His authorship lies in constructing possibility spaces and exclusions, not withdrawing from decision.
4. Physical prints and drawings do not merely reproduce software; they disclose resolution, density, duration, and material trace differently.
5. Processing and Feral File matter because they extend studio values—legibility, iteration, access, peer exchange—into shared infrastructures, but they are not interchangeable with the artworks.
6. The move into blockchain is continuous with earlier questions but materially changes edition, instantiation, distribution, ownership, and public comparison.
7. Transparency of rule can coexist with perceptual opacity; viewers may know the system and still confront fatigue or illegibility.
8. Reas's work has repeatedly moved between endogenous systems and source-image systems: artificial agents and Process on one side; broadcast, cinema, photography, and ML datasets on the other.
9. The seven-work Museum group is strongest as a longitudinal argument built from recent tokens that reach backward into older systems, not as a survey of all media.
10. The gift's institutional significance lies in transferring a coherent study group into public trust and accepting its preservation obligations, not in market status.

## 11. Required omissions to acknowledge in the monograph and collection essay

The Museum group contains:

- three works from the 2021 Art Blocks CENTURY project;
- one Pre-Process;
- one Phototaxis;
- one 923 EMPTY ROOMS;
- one Ex Nihilo (Cosmos).

It does not contain:

- an early Path, Tissue, or MicroImage print/software installation;
- a Software Structures implementation;
- a Process text, print, software work, or installation;
- a Processing archive or edition;
- an Ultraconcentrated / Signal to Noise work;
- an A Mathematical Theory of Communication work;
- a Compressed Cinema still or video;
- an In Silico work;
- a physical print, plotter drawing, woodblock, book, sculpture, or installation component;
- a representative work from every major body.

These absences are future collecting opportunities and interpretive limits. They do not invalidate the accession.

# Technical and condition review

**Accession lot:** `6529NM.2026.001`
**Review date:** 2026-08-02
**Scope:** seven Casey REAS Art Blocks works, `6529NM.2026.001.01` through `.07`
**Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum, Collection Care and Technical Conservation
**Decision authority:** direct Museum-authorized collection authority recorded in `6529NM.2026.001.GAA-01`

## Outcome

The lot passes technical and condition review with conditions. All seven objects are suitable for accession and for noncommercial Museum display through the current official Art Blocks generator routes, provided the display identifies the live network and browser dependencies and carries the approved attribution. No red condition is present. Software preservation remains in progress and is managed as continuing stewardship, not as an unanswered accession review.

## Reviewed findings

| Domain | Rating | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token and custody | Green | Contract, token ID, CAIP-19 identity, transfer transaction, block, log, destination, and current custody are verified and mutually joined. |
| Metadata | Green | Exact Art Blocks metadata response bytes are retained with SHA-256 fixity and object-specific source bindings. The live endpoint remains externally operated, but the accession evidence does not depend on its future availability. |
| Script/generator | Amber | All seven official generator URLs were available and produced changing renderable output. The complete assembled generator and project-script byte set has not yet been retained in a self-contained Museum preservation package. |
| Dependencies | Amber | The six `CENTURY`, `Pre-Process`, `Phototaxis`, and `923 EMPTY ROOMS` records identify p5.js 1.0.0 via cdnjs; the `Ex Nihilo (Cosmos)` record identifies p5.js 1.9.0 via cdnjs. A complete dependency lockfile and locally executable dependency bundle are not yet retained. |
| Rendering | Amber | Each official generator rendered successfully in the recorded viewport observation. Browser version, user agent, exact frame timestamps, and a second independent render environment were not fixed. |
| Behavior | Amber | Two successive frames differed for every object, establishing observed live change but not full interaction coverage, timing semantics, or determinism. Documented keyboard controls were not exhaustively exercised. |
| Documentation | Amber | Raw metadata, hashes, dimensions, byte counts, source URLs, object descriptions, and two-frame observations are retained. The previously observed image and screenshot bytes themselves are not in the public repository. Their noncommercial retention is now rights-cleared and is an active preservation action. |
| Preservation | Amber | The content-addressed evidence package, recovery lineage, chain evidence, and collection-wide descriptors are retained. Self-contained generator/dependency capture and two-environment reproducibility remain in progress. |
| Display | Ready with conditions | Current official generators may be used for noncommercial display with CC BY-NC 4.0 attribution, network/browser dependency disclosure, a tested fallback, and monitoring during exhibition. |

These ratings are deliberately asymmetric. Verified object identity and retained metadata fixity are green even though the works are not yet preserved as autonomous executable packages. The generator and render findings are amber, rather than red, because the object-specific official routes were available and produced changing output in the controlled observation. They are not green because that observation does not establish an independently executable Museum copy, complete dependencies, reproducibility across environments, or future-browser behavior. A later failure of the official route before local capture would trigger immediate reassessment and may justify a red rating.

## Object-specific findings

- **CENTURY #31, #724, and #401:** the retained metadata and token identity are complete. The observed routes use p5.js 1.0.0 via cdnjs, and the two-frame checks establish changing live output. The reviewed scripts bind `1` to cut/reorder and `2` to restore the ordered composition. Those controls were not exercised in the retained observations. All three remain amber for behavior, generator capture, and reproducibility.
- **Pre-Process #63:** the p5.js 1.0.0 official generator rendered and changed across the two observed frames. The reviewed interaction map is mouse press to reset; `1`–`8` to select a surface and reset; space to reset; and `P` to pause/resume. Before preservation is marked complete, test orientation, every reset path, frame-rate and duration effects, and whether repeated execution returns to an equivalent initial state.
- **Phototaxis #308:** the p5.js 1.0.0 official generator rendered and changed. Artist-documented controls (`P`, `B`, `1`–`5`, `L`) and the described 1,000-frame stopping behavior were not exercised in the retained observation, so behavior remains amber.
- **923 EMPTY ROOMS #713:** the p5.js 1.0.0 official generator rendered and changed. The retained population contains 924 invocations numbered `0`–`923`; invocation `0` is separately coded `999999`, while invocations `1`–`923` are the documented combinatorial sequence. The reviewed generator contains the same 924-entry table. Token `1000713` is invocation `713` and maps to `Code=555536`. This resolves the numerical structure but not the artistic meaning of invocation zero. Script, shader, controls, and state behavior remain preservation-completion work, not accession blockers.
- **Ex Nihilo (Cosmos) #248:** the p5.js 1.9.0 official generator rendered and changed. Space generates a new state; `P` pauses/resumes; `S` changes speed; `G` and `W` toggle implemented display states; and lowercase `r` and `b` toggle the implemented red and blue states. The generator contains duplicated lowercase comparisons, so the uppercase `R` and `B` instructions in platform metadata are not implemented as written. This is an amber behavior/documentation discrepancy, not a red accession defect. Exhibition instructions must follow the tested implementation and disclose the difference.

## Source-reviewed interaction maps

These maps transcribe the reviewed project scripts and artist/platform instructions. They are complete as source documentation at accession; the retained visual observations did not exhaustively exercise them, so behavior remains amber until controlled interaction testing is complete.

| Work | Inputs and actions |
| --- | --- |
| CENTURY | `1`: cut and reorder image slices; `2`: restore the ordered composition. |
| Pre-Process | Mouse press: reset; `1`–`8`: select surface and reset; space: reset; `P`: pause/resume. |
| Phototaxis | `P`: pause/resume; `B`: restart; `1`–`5`: change magnification; `L`: reveal/hide light locations; automatic stop after 1,000 iterations for the initial thumbnail state. |
| 923 EMPTY ROOMS | `+`/`-`: scale; `D`: diagram; space: background state; `R`/`G`/`B`: color channels; `1`–`6`: city presets; arrows: depth; `S`: speed; `0`/`9`: line length; `T`: resolution; `P`: save current view. |
| Ex Nihilo (Cosmos) | Space: new state; `P`: pause/resume; `S`: speed; `G`/`W`: implemented display toggles; lowercase `r`/`b`: implemented red/blue toggles. Platform documentation's uppercase `R`/`B` differs from the reviewed code. |

## Display specification

For each exhibition, the Museum must record the date, generator URI, browser and version, operating system, viewport and backing resolution, network requirement, interaction mode, and whether the work is shown live or through a labelled documentation surrogate. Test the exact installation before opening and after material browser, operating-system, generator, or dependency changes. Monitor network-backed live displays and maintain a rights-compliant fallback capture or recording. Do not present a still as the complete software work; label it as a documentation surrogate.

## Active preservation actions

The following actions are approved and required. They are not pending reviews:

1. Retain rights-compliant static and live documentation bytes with fixity and attribution.
2. Capture the exact project scripts, assembled generators, dependency assets, and on-chain inputs for each object.
3. Record a reproducible render environment and verify each object in at least two materially distinct browser/operating-system environments.
4. Exercise and document artist- or platform-described controls, timing behavior, and reset semantics.
5. Assign at least two durable replicas outside the live serving path and run periodic fixity and recovery tests.
6. Reassess after any material contract, metadata, generator, browser, dependency, custody, or display change.

Accession is complete at the reviewed amber condition. `Preservation complete`, `technically verified`, and `display ready` remain later workflow states only when their stricter evidence gates are met.

# Title, rights, and accession review

**Accession lot:** `6529NM.2026.001`
**Decision date:** 2026-08-02
**Acquisition method:** gift
**Donor credit:** punk6529
**Objects reviewed:** seven Casey REAS Art Blocks tokens, `6529NM.2026.001.01` through `.07`
**Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum, Registrar
**Decision authority:** direct Museum-authorized collection authority recorded in `6529NM.2026.001.GAA-01`

## Determination

The 6529 Network Museum determines that the seven scheduled tokens are eligible for and accepted into the permanent collection. The donor made a full gift: the Museum accepts the donor's entire ownership interest in the tokens and every donor-held interest that is transferable with them, without consideration and without a retained donor interest. The common Ethereum transfer into `networkmuseum.6529.eth`, the exact contract/token schedule, the Museum's formal gift acceptance, and this reviewed title declaration together establish a sufficient title basis for accession.

This determination does not collapse token ownership into copyright ownership. The Museum owns the seven tokenized collection objects. No copyright assignment from Casey REAS is asserted or inferred. Copyright and similar rights remain with the applicable licensor or rights holder except to the extent exercised under the public license attached to each work's retained Art Blocks metadata.

The Museum accepts the ordinary residual risk that a public blockchain cannot disclose every possible private claim, security interest, incapacity, or off-chain dispute. No contrary claim, competing on-chain owner, consideration, donor reservation, or object-identity conflict is present in the reviewed record. That residual limitation is documented and accepted; it is not an open accession gate.

## Evidence and title analysis

The title conclusion rests on four mutually reinforcing records:

1. The donor's instruction, treated by the Museum as a full and intentional gift of all donor-held interests in the seven tokens.
2. The formally accepted [Gift Acceptance and Accession Authorization](gift-acceptance-authorization.md), made under the adopted Art Blocks preapproval and Donation Acceptance Policy.
3. Ethereum transaction `0xbdde33b32d4b70335b10cbd37c0b00a027844f14c900d82aa4f75b7a7b390498`, whose seven ERC-721 `Transfer` logs deliver the exact scheduled assets to the Museum custody address.
4. The object-level chain identities, transaction log indices, and custody findings in the machine records and retained raw RPC receipt.

The transfer transaction is both custody evidence and performance of the gift. The institutional title declaration does not pretend to be a donor-signed deed; it records the Museum's reviewed conclusion from the donor's full-gift declaration, completed delivery, formal acceptance, and exact object schedule. The Museum considers that evidence sufficient for these no-consideration token gifts under its donation pathway.

The provenance record is complete for the accession event and exact receipt. Earlier token history may be enriched through continuing scholarship, but the absence of a prose ownership history for every prior wallet is not an accession blocker where the object identity, donor gift, delivery, and current custody are verified and no adverse claim is known.

## Copyright and public-license analysis

All seven retained Art Blocks metadata responses identify the artist as Casey REAS and state `CC BY-NC 4.0`. The Museum treats those labels as object-specific source evidence that the licensed material is offered under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International Public License. Under the [official legal code](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/legalcode.en), the license grants worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive, irrevocable permission to reproduce and share the licensed material and to produce, reproduce, and share adapted material for noncommercial purposes. It permits all media and formats and technical modifications needed to exercise those rights. The [official deed](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/deed.en) summarizes the same permissions and principal conditions.

The Museum therefore makes the following affirmative use determinations:

| Use | Determination | Conditions and boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exhibition and public display | Granted with conditions | Museum use must be noncommercial, attributed, linked to the license and source where practicable, and must not imply artist endorsement. |
| Reproduction and documentation | Granted with conditions | Noncommercial captures, thumbnails, stills, video documentation, and study copies may be made and shared with the required notices. |
| Publication | Granted with conditions | Noncommercial collection pages, catalogues, scholarship, educational material, and social communication are permitted with attribution and license notice. |
| Print | Granted with conditions | Noncommercial labels, study prints, conservation references, and publications are permitted; commercial merchandise is not authorized by this record. |
| Derivative and adapted use | Granted with conditions | Noncommercial adaptations are permitted; changes and prior modifications must be identified, and an adapter's terms may not prevent compliance with CC BY-NC 4.0. |
| Preservation copying | Granted with conditions | The Museum may retain source, generator, dependency, render, migration, emulation, and recovery copies for noncommercial stewardship and may make necessary technical modifications. |
| Migration and emulation | Granted with conditions | Technical modifications necessary for lawful noncommercial use are permitted; material changes must be documented when the result is shared. |
| Accessibility | Granted with conditions | Noncommercial accessible renditions and interpretive adaptations are permitted with attribution and change marking. |
| AI training and computational research | Granted with conditions | To the extent copyright permission is required, the Museum may reproduce or adapt the licensed material for its own noncommercial research, cataloguing, conservation, and analysis. This record does not authorize commercial model training or waive rights outside the license. |

Commercial use is not granted by CC BY-NC 4.0 and is not approved by this review. Patent and trademark rights are not licensed. Moral, publicity, privacy, and similar rights are not broadly licensed, although the legal code contains a limited waiver or non-assertion to the extent necessary to exercise the licensed rights. The license supplies no warranty of title or non-infringement. Uses independently permitted by an exception or limitation remain outside the license's conditions.

## Attribution and use protocol

Whenever the Museum shares a work or an adapted version, the accompanying credit must, so far as supplied and reasonably practicable:

- identify Casey REAS as creator and preserve any other supplied attribution party;
- identify the work and its Museum accession number;
- state `CC BY-NC 4.0` and link to `https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/`;
- link to the source object or official project record where reasonably practicable;
- retain supplied copyright and warranty-disclaimer notices;
- state whether the Museum modified the material and preserve notice of earlier modifications; and
- avoid any suggestion that Casey REAS, Art Blocks, or another attribution party endorses the Museum or a particular use.

Recommended collection credit: `Casey REAS, [title], [year]; on-chain generative software associated with an Ethereum ERC-721 token; 6529 Network Museum, gift of punk6529, [accession number]. Licensed CC BY-NC 4.0.` Add `Museum documentation capture` or a precise change statement to derivatives and surrogates.

## Registrar and risk conclusions

- **Identity and authenticity:** pass. Exact CAIP-19 identities, token hashes where supplied, Art Blocks project data, raw metadata bytes, and the common transfer receipt are fixed in the evidence package.
- **Donor authority and title:** pass with accepted residual risk. The Museum relies on the donor's full-gift declaration and completed delivery; no adverse claim or donor reservation is recorded.
- **Provenance:** pass for accession. The accession transfer is fully documented in the Stream-compatible provenance schedule; earlier chain history remains ordinary cataloguing enrichment.
- **Rights:** pass with conditions. The Museum owns the tokens, not the artist's copyright; the object-specific CC BY-NC 4.0 grant supports the noncommercial museum uses listed above.
- **Compliance:** pass. The gift involved no consideration, no restricted material, no personal-data payload, and no identified sanctions, dispute, or encumbrance indicator in the reviewed record. The limits of public wallet evidence are accepted rather than mislabeled as certainty.
- **Curatorial case:** pass. The artist profile, collection essay, and object records establish the significance of the artist, the projects, the seven works, and the collection's fit with the Museum's mission without converting interpretation into artist intent.

## Accession outcome

Title, rights, identity, provenance, curatorial significance, condition, and technical evidence are sufficient for accession. The lot is approved for the permanent collection as `accessioned`. Long-term software preservation, dependency capture, multi-environment rendering, periodic custody verification, and future provenance enrichment remain active stewardship duties. They do not postpone the accession decision.

# Curatorial accession review: Conflict at Its Edges

Conflict at Its Edges brings together five photographs from Magnum Photos 75:
David Seymour's patrol at the Negev border; Larry Towell's soldiers in a
church in Suchitoto; Micha Bar-Am's demonstration at the Western Wall; Moisés
Saman's damaged room in Tripoli; and Lorenzo Meloni's view of Palmyra after its
recapture. The group moves across decades and geographies, but its coherence is
not simply the presence of conflict. It is the way each image tests the distance
between an event and its representation.

The photographs attend to edges: territorial borders, a threshold between
military presence and religious space, the crowd and the wall, a room after an
air strike, and a site encountered after destruction. Their subjects are not
offered as interchangeable evidence or as a complete history of any conflict.
The group asks what a photograph can establish, what its caption supplies, and
what remains beyond the frame.

The Museum has accessioned the five works as one coherent curatorial group. The
individual object records preserve the source captions, artist credits,
technical observations, and unresolved claims. Together they form an accession
that can be studied as a set without collapsing the differences among the
photographers, assignments, places, and moments.

# Technical and condition review

The five accession objects are ERC-721 tokens with photographic source images.
The Museum verified each transfer receipt and matching Transfer log, read
ownerOf at the common finalized Ethereum block 25741809, and retained the
source metadata and image references from the proposal package.

The objects are ready for credited accession-context display. Their source
images are not yet asserted to be Museum preservation masters. Image-byte
retention, redundant replication, rights-compliant display, and further
provenance enrichment remain active stewardship actions. No executable artwork,
generator, or software dependency is asserted for these photographic objects.

# Title, rights, and accession review

**Accession lot:** 6529NM.2026.002  
**Gift:** Conflict at Its Edges, five photographs from Magnum Photos 75  
**Donor:** punk6529  
**Status:** accepted and accessioned into the permanent Collection

## Title basis

The donor offered the five scheduled tokens as a full gift. The Museum
maintainer instructed the Museum to record the gift as accepted and accessioned.
The five transfer receipts identify delivery from the donor address to
networkmuseum.6529.eth; the custody package records the receipts, their
Transfer logs, and the common finalized-block ownerOf observation.

The Museum's title record therefore covers the donor's transferable interest in
the five tokenized objects. This public record derives that determination from
the full-gift offer and the maintainer's instruction. It does not cite a
separate private instrument.

## Rights position

The source records identify the photographs as All Rights Reserved and credit
each artist and Magnum Photos. The gift transfers the tokenized objects and the
donor's transferable interest in them; it does not transfer copyright or
create a general reproduction licence. The Museum's public presentation is
limited to the credited accession context and remains subject to the source
rights position.

## Supporting records

- Gift acceptance and accession authorization
- Accession certificate
- Finalized custody evidence
- Source and rights record

# Web presentation of *Conflict at Its Edges*

The 6529 Network Museum acquired the five tokenized photographs in *Conflict at Its Edges* and interprets that acquisition as carrying the ordinary institutional right to display and publish the works in a credited Museum context. Copyright remains with the photographers and Magnum Photos. The Museum does not claim copyright ownership or a general licence to reproduce, sell, sublicense, download, alter, or train models on the images.

For a practical and accessible web presentation, the Museum may produce proportion-preserving delivery copies from each fixity-verified source image. The approved technical process applies EXIF orientation, converts embedded colour profiles to sRGB or treats an untagged source as sRGB, resizes with Lanczos filtering, and encodes WebP copies at 640, 1280, and 2400 pixels wide. It does not crop, watermark, retouch, recolour, or otherwise alter the depicted content.

Within this accession context, this authority supersedes the proposal-stage delivery rule that barred Museum responsive variants. That earlier rule remains part of the proposal's historical record; this authority does not alter the recorded source objects or their underlying rights.

The exact Arweave image remains the recorded source object. Every web copy is identified by its source hash, transform profile, dimensions, byte size, and its own SHA-256 digest. The browser receives the smallest appropriate copy for its viewport; the source original is not the default page payload. These delivery copies are display surrogates, not preservation masters and not downloadable publication assets.

Each display must retain the work's artist, title, date or place where recorded, Magnum credit, All Rights Reserved notice, and accession context. This authority applies to the Museum's own public site and records. It creates no permission for third-party reuse.

# A field of practice

- **Subtitle:** Collecting, presenting, and caring for digital art
- **Series:** A field of practice

## Contents

[Overview](#overview) · [Selection method](#selection-method) · [Thematic pathways](#thematic-pathways) · [Working lessons](#working-lessons) · [Profiles by question](#profiles-by-question) · [Related research](#related-research) · [Revision history](#revision-history)

## Overview

An encounter with [Douglas Davis's *The World's First Collaborative Sentence*](profiles/whitney.md)
can involve a live contribution surface, a restored historical state, broken
links, and malformed Korean characters. Rhizome's record of [*My Boyfriend Came
Back From the War*](profiles/rhizome-new-museum.md) asks a related question at
the level of the browser: nested frames divide the screen, clicking changes the
composition, and variant history records the access environment. These cases
establish the study's starting point: a digital artwork
requires a record of what it does, where it runs, which state a reader
encounters, and what changed during care.

The study follows four connected questions:

1. How is a digital work identified when its behavior depends on a runtime,
   browser, network, device, or service?
2. Which changes count as intervention, migration, reconstruction, or loss?
3. How can a collection record open paths to research, correction, citation,
   and reuse?
4. Which parts of a method depend on specific labor, rights, budgets, or
   technical infrastructure?

Profiles are grouped by the museum problem they illuminate and arranged as a
reading sequence.

## Selection method

The study comprises twenty-seven case files. Selection is case-based. A profile enters
when public primary institutional material documents a work, project, record,
archive, conservation action, technical tool, commission, or research
publication that bears directly on digital art or on a transferable museum
record problem.

Each case must provide:

- a named anchor work, project, record, or institutional artifact;
- a concrete action or record structure that a reader can inspect;
- a documented limit, dependency, omission, unresolved state, or change
  history;
- exact source titles, dates, access information, and claim-level links; and
- a reason the evidence matters to the Museum's collection, publication,
  preservation, rights, or public-access work.

Mission statements establish stated purpose. Collection records, work pages,
archives, conservation studies, datasets, technical documentation, research
publications, and program records establish demonstrated practice. A profile
may therefore describe an ongoing or partial method without presenting it as a
completed institutional capability.

The study excludes prestige, collection size, visitor numbers, awards,
marketplace metrics, generic technology claims, and institutional promotion as
selection grounds. Broad institutional history appears only when it explains a
specific record, work, decision, or dependency. Each profile is limited to the
documented practice and sources named on its page.

## Working lessons

### Describe the encounter before the interpretation

Every digital-work record should state what the work does and what the reader
must use to encounter it: interface, runtime, browser or device, network,
interaction, duration, sound, display state, and known access limits.

### Separate identity, manifestation, and intervention

Keep a stable work identity beside dated manifestations and intervention
events. A live version, historical capture, emulation, migration, restoration,
and static documentation surrogate should remain distinguishable.

### Publish loss and missingness

Record unavailable dependencies, broken links, incomplete captures, encoding
defects, service closures, artificial ordering, and unresolved rights. State
what was observed, what was reconstructed, and what remains inaccessible.

### Connect the object to its research paths

Stable identifiers should connect the accessioned work to artist, project,
manifestation, provenance, rights, conservation, technical, exhibition,
bibliographic, source, and revision records. A public page should lead to the
supporting record without making the interface carry the record's full
durability burden.

### Record operational responsibility

Publish the roles, authority, method, test conditions, access permissions,
dependencies, and rights that shaped a work's presentation or preservation.
The record should identify the decision and the evidence behind it.

### Keep revisions visible

Every substantial publication should carry version, date, research cutoff,
source state, correction route, and supersession history. A stronger account
should extend the record while preserving the earlier assertion and the reason
for the change.

### Test transfer at the field level

For each case, the study identifies the field, form, workflow, source path, or
record relationship the Museum could adapt. It also states the work that
adaptation would require and the dependency that limits the comparison.

The word “museum” does too much work around digital and blockchain art. A
platform may publish an artwork without owning it. A marketplace may record a
sale without establishing provenance. A festival may distribute a work without
collecting it. A DAO may coordinate participation without holding legal
authority. A token may identify an edition without preserving its runtime,
rights, or public history. This essay therefore classifies each precedent by
what its public work demonstrates, not by the institution’s preferred label.
Official pages establish what an organization says and publishes; they do not,
without further evidence, establish custody, title, preservation, or public
authority.

Selection confers no rank. The practices answer different Museum problems.
Feral File and Art Blocks are useful for exhibition interfaces and
technical identity. Bright Moments and Verse document event, release, and
market mechanisms. DAM and MoRE address artist records, collection scope,
rights, and public scholarship. DiMoDA and the Museum of Other Realities
show native-runtime presentation. MOCA, Furtherfield, and The Wrong document
community and distributed programs without proving decentralized collection
governance. DATALAND documents a dynamic AI/data exhibition, while 0xCollection
shows how a private experiential initiative can make non-documentation part of
its curatorial position.

## Platforms and chain-native systems

### Feral File

Feral File describes itself as a cultural institution and technology company.
Its [“Curator’s Note | FF1”](https://feralfile.com/retrospective/ff1/curators-note/)
is dated 9 June 2023 and presents exhibitions as persistent online
publications. [“One to Zero”](https://feralfile.com/exhibitions/shows/one-to-zero-bti)
places a curator’s note beside artist, title, year, series, medium,
dimensions, duration, generative or interactive fields, and smart-contract
information. The [Feral File documentation](https://docs.feralfile.com/)
publishes DP-1 protocol and API material. Its [“How to Collect Digital
Art”](https://feralfile.com/learn/how-to-collect-digital-art) guide separates
the token from artwork files, rights agreements, hashes, storage, and
dependencies.

The prose moves from curatorial premise to concise object record. That is a
useful public catalogue pattern, but the reviewed pages do not provide a
public Museum accession, condition, title, or custody system. “Preservation”
and “stewarded collections” remain institutional descriptions unless supported
by public recovery, intervention, and service-dependency records.

The Museum should adopt a curator’s note as an interpretive layer and keep
exhibition, artist, artwork, edition, contract, rights, and technical
dependency records distinct. It should not treat platform publication,
collector ownership, pricing, or the persistence of a URL as accession,
provenance, or preservation. Art Computer, Art Panel, collector workflows, and
platform fees are commercially specific.

### Art Blocks

[“About Art Blocks”](https://www.artblocks.io/articles/about-art-blocks) is
dated 27 November 2020. It describes a platform in which purchasing a token
triggers execution of an artist’s generative code. The [protocol
overview](https://docs.artblocks.io/protocol/overview/), [“Core Contract
(V3)”](https://docs.artblocks.io/developer/core-contract/), and [GraphQL
reference](https://docs.artblocks.io/developer/graphql/) expose project IDs,
scripts, token hashes, dependencies, royalties, contract controls, and
queryable entities. [“PostParams”](https://docs.artblocks.io/protocol/postparams/)
documents mutable token parameters and live-data behavior. [“NFT Metadata
Storage at Art Blocks”](https://docs.artblocks.io/protocol/on-chain-storage/)
also states limitations involving blockchain continuity and future access.

Art Blocks writes primarily as technical documentation. It explains how a work
is generated, identified, rendered, configured, sold, and queried. The Museum
should adopt that precision: record contract, token, chain, mint transaction,
script or seed hash, dependency source and version, renderer, runtime,
external assets, mutable parameters, administrative authority, upgradeability,
and reproducibility results.

The technical boundary is specific. On-chain code and contract data do not
automatically preserve browsers, operating systems, hardware, external assets,
APIs, artist documentation, legal rights, or public access. Platform tiers,
royalties, primary sales, and white-label Engine licensing are commercial
infrastructure. Determinism is an evidence-bearing property of a work, not a
conclusion that preservation is complete.

### Bright Moments

Bright Moments describes itself as producing live, on-chain, in-person art
experiences and as being organized as a DAO through CryptoCitizens on its
[“About” page](https://www.brightmoments.io/about). Its [“Where Art is
Born” archive](https://www.brightmoments.io/archive) records city programs,
artists, algorithmic collections, and live minting. Its [retrospective
site](https://www.brightmoments.io/) and [“Mint Pass
Policy”](https://docs.brightmoments.io/policies/mint-pass-policy) describe the
project's history and participation mechanics.

Its publication style is event-driven: history pages, artist lists, city
narratives, FAQs, and participation policies. The archive can help reconstruct
where and when a work was minted or revealed, but it is not object-level
scholarship or condition documentation. The Museum should create separate
records for event, city, venue, producer or curator, artist, algorithm,
contract, mint/reveal conditions, visitor access, and documentation state.

A live mint is an event, not an accession. A CryptoCitizen token is a
membership or identity instrument, not evidence of Museum authority or legal
title. Token-gated access, city membership, and event revenue should not be
copied as institutional practice.

### Verse

[Verse Documentation](https://docs.verse.works/) describes release, collection,
contract, sale, access-control, API, and GraphQL models. The [curatorial
board](https://verse.works/board) identifies named curatorial participants.
[“This Is Tomorrow: Part III”](https://verse.works/exhibitions/this-is-tomorrow-part-3)
presents curator-selected works with artist, nominator, edition, price, and
descriptive prose. [“Contract Basics”](https://docs.verse.works/contract/basics/)
distinguishes artist-owned contracts from temporary Verse mint permissions.
The official [“Terms”](https://verse.works/terms) frame Verse as a centralized
marketplace and set limits around authenticity, provenance, and intellectual
property.

Verse’s writing is a hybrid of exhibition essay and sales catalogue. The
selection chain is visible because curators and nominators are named, but
price, edition, release, and purchase remain central. The Museum should record
who selected, nominated, commissioned, minted, sold, or held a work and should
separate exhibition interpretation from sale data.

A listing, price, edition, or secondary sale is not accession evidence. A
marketplace’s legal disclaimer is not a Museum provenance policy. Custodial
wallets, payment rails, and secondary-market data are platform functions, not
condition or preservation records.

## Archives, publication bodies, and native-runtime presentation

### DAM — Digital Art Museum

DAM is an online digital-art resource associated with DAM Projects GmbH; its
[imprint](https://dam.org/museum/dam/imprint/) identifies the publisher and
warns that the site is not necessarily complete or current. The [Vera Molnar
record](https://dam.org/museum/artists_ui/artists/molnar-vera/) combines series,
biography, artist statement, references, publications, exhibitions, and
chronology. The [Casey Reas record](https://dam.org/museum/artists_ui/artists/reas-casey/)
distinguishes instructions, systems, source code, executable form, and
manifestation. The [“Frieder Nake Reflects on 60 Years of Algorithmic
Art”](https://dam.org/museum/essays_ui/essays/frieder-nake-wolf-lieser-60-years-of-algorithmic-art/)
essay is dated 11 November 2025.

DAM offers a useful artist-centered publication model. The Museum should
retain primary artist language, series chronology, references, and the
distinction between an artwork’s system and a particular manifestation. DAM
does not provide chain custody or public accession evidence, and its
copyright and commercial relationship mean that its material should not be
assumed openly reusable.

## Artist-led data museum and private experiential collection

### DATALAND

DATALAND describes itself as a museum and digital ecosystem on its
[“About” page](https://dataland.art/about). Its [“Dataland: Living

The exhibition record is a useful dossier for dynamic work. 6529 should record

The limit is authority. “Living museum,” “ethical data,” and “comprehensive

## What the Museum should implement

The comparative material supports a narrow set of concrete changes:

1. **Classify relations before interpreting them.** Use distinct relation types
   for accession, donation, commission, exhibition, platform publication,
   sale, mint/reveal event, community selection, archive capture, technical
   dependency, and rights instrument.
2. **Add a chain-native technical layer.** Record CAIP-19-shaped identity,
   contract, token or edition, mint evidence, script or seed hash, dependency
   versions, renderer, runtime, external assets, mutable parameters, authority,
   upgradeability, and reproducibility results.
3. **Keep authority layers separate.** Token identity, transfer history, legal
   title, custody, copyright, display rights, preservation rights, and Museum
   accession are different assertions.
4. **Publish in layers.** A stable object record should lead to a curatorial
   essay, provenance and rights history, technical and condition records,
   bibliography, machine-readable data, and a correction route.
5. **Record program conditions.** For live, distributed, or native-runtime
   work, record venue, device, software, event, curator, selection method,
   access state, documentation limits, and failure mode.
6. **State limitations where they change meaning.** “On-chain,” “permanent,”
   “decentralized,” “living,” and “preserved” must be tied to the specific
   component and evidence that supports the term.

These lessons extend the existing Museum standards without changing their
authority rules. A platform page can open a research path; it cannot replace
the accession record. A protocol can expose technical identity; it cannot
replace a condition report. A festival can preserve program history; it cannot
convert participation into title. A token can identify an edition; it cannot
carry the whole work’s rights, runtime, or institutional memory.

# ACMI — Collecting and Preserving Screen Culture

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

ACMI's [Microgames Commission](https://www.acmi.net.au/collection-preservation/commissions/microgame/) makes the obligations of a collecting museum concrete. The creator retains full rights; ACMI receives a playable copy and source code for its archive, permission to exhibit, and a record of preservation intentions and display parameters. The commission therefore joins legal status, executable materials, and future access without treating them as one fact.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Acquisition and accession are different records

The [ACMI Collection Strategy 2024–2029](https://www.acmi.net.au/collection-preservation/strategy/) distinguishes acquisition, accession, cataloguing, data, preservation, access, loans, storage, and deaccessioning. Acquisition transfers title through an agreement; accession follows approval, agreement, and receipt of materials. Cataloguing records interpretation, rights, creator, technical information, and management events such as display, storage, movement, loan, and preservation.

This vocabulary prevents a commission, loan, or public display from becoming an implied accession. It also gives a public record a place for technical and administrative events that would otherwise disappear into prose.

### 2. Commission terms carry preservation information

The Microgames page names the rights position, the archive package, exhibition permission, an exclusivity period, and the conversation through which ACMI records preservation intentions and display parameters. The playable copy and source code are related materials with different future uses: one supports access, while the other supports study and preservation.

The Museum should use the same distinction for executable works. A record should identify the constitutive package, the display package, the rights granted, and the evidence for each. It should not infer ownership from possession of a file.

### 3. Research display is not collection status

ACMI's [*Play It Again 2: Preserving Australian Videogames*](https://www.acmi.net.au/works/119969--play-it-again-2-preserving-australian-videogames/) describes disk imaging, emulation, developer and player interviews, and access research. The page also states that the works presented are not in ACMI's collection. That sentence is an important control: research, exhibition, and collection management remain visible as separate relationships.

### 4. Preservation method is published as a sequence

The [time-based media preservation resource](https://www.acmi.net.au/education/school-program-and-resources/exhibiting-preservation-and-conservation-of-time-based-media-art/) moves from acquisition interview through appraisal, identification, authenticity, fixity, characterisation, significant properties, preservation metadata, and access. Its case discussion of generative work asks what should be retained about source code, software, hardware, executables, versions, behavior, interaction, and display.

## Publication and scholarship

ACMI's strategy establishes a controlled vocabulary; its commission page translates that vocabulary into artist-facing terms; its preservation resource turns institutional casework into a public procedure; and its videogame project records a boundary between research display and collection. The writing is most useful when it names the status of a thing before explaining its significance.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Record acquisition, accession, exhibition, research, loan, and hosted status separately.
- Request source code, executable or playable material, dependencies, display parameters, preservation intentions, and fixity evidence where relevant.
- Link creator rights and exhibition permission to the exact agreement or record.
- Publish preservation work as a dated sequence of observations, decisions, interventions, and unresolved differences.
- Use an explicit “not in collection” state when research or display does not establish accession.

## Where the analogy ends

ACMI's source-code deposit is an agreement-specific archive arrangement, not proof that ACMI owns the work. Its lab, staffing, public mandate, and physical storage cannot be reproduced at equivalent scale by the 6529 Network Museum. The transferable practice is the separation of status, materials, rights, and preservation evidence.

# Ars Electronica

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The Ars Electronica Festival began in 1979, the Prix Ars Electronica in 1987,
and the Ars Electronica Center and Futurelab in 1996. The institution now
describes its organization as an ecosystem comprising festival, award, museum,
archive, laboratory, and client-facing Solutions work. The dates are
institutional history; “ecosystem” is the institution’s own organizational
description. [About Ars Electronica](https://ars.electronica.art/about/en/) · [History – Ars Electronica Futurelab](https://ars.electronica.art/futurelab/en/about/history/) · [Organization](https://ars.electronica.art/about/en/organization/)

## Project record: Spaxels

The Futurelab’s *Spaxels* page dates the project’s main development and
performances from 2012 to 2017. It identifies the 2012 Linz commission,
explains “Spaxel” as a space-based picture element, describes centrally
controlled and choreographed drone formations, and follows the work through
later projects, Fluxels, and the swarms+art platform. [Spaxels](https://ars.electronica.art/futurelab/en/projects-spaxels/)

The page joins origin, mechanism, aesthetic rationale, collaborators, later
iterations, and related research. It documents project history and public
presentation. Title, custody, rights, and permanent collection status require
separate evidence.

## An archive with technical depth

Ars Electronica’s archive documents more than four decades of festivals,
projects, exhibitions, awards, publications, and media-art activity. Its own
account reports approximately 60,000 physical records, more than 210,000
digital entries, and 68 terabytes. Database records and files are automatically
transferred to and tested in a backup system, with additional tape backup.
Access is public where legal and technical conditions allow. [About the Ars Electronica Archive](https://ars.electronica.art/archive/en/about/)

The online archive makes Prix submissions searchable across years and
categories, documents winning projects with audiovisual and textual material,
and provides publications, photographs, videos, a Prix map, and project
histories. [Ars Electronica Archive](https://ars.electronica.art/archive/en/)

Ars Electronica also preserves earlier versions of its public web presence by
converting historical sites into static, compatible versions, repairing broken
links where possible, and adding current websites for research. These are
preservation copies with stated limits on original behavior. [Websites](https://ars.electronica.art/archive/en/websites/)

## Research made public

The Ars Electronica Center describes exhibition and laboratory spaces as a
shared research environment for artists, scientists, and visitors. Its
research page specifically identifies Deep Space 8K as a site for work on
digital avatars, virtual reality, and human–robot scenarios. [Researching the Future](https://ars.electronica.art/center/en/researching-the-future/)

The Futurelab makes selected project documentation, papers, publications,
research reports, patents, and code available through its public platform.
[Ars Electronica Futurelab](https://ars.electronica.art/futurelab/en/)
The platform therefore exposes some process artifacts alongside project
descriptions; the available materials remain project-specific and do not form a
complete technical record for every work.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Give every program event its own record: call, eligibility review, selection,
  jury decision, presentation, archive inclusion, acquisition, and accession.
  Link the records without treating one state as proof of another.
- Snapshot each public collection or program site at release, retaining the
  URL, timestamp, capture format, source revision, repaired links, and known
  losses.
- Publish preservation scripts, contract prototypes, and exhibition adapters
  with their version, inputs, outputs, assumptions, and affected works.
- Maintain redundant copies with an explicit access matrix distinguishing
  public, rights-restricted, technically unavailable, and preservation-only
  material.
- Keep awards, archive inclusion, public presentation, title, custody, rights,
  and accession as separate fields and decisions.

## Where the analogy ends

Ars Electronica combines a museum, festival, competition, laboratory,
education programs, and client work through Ars Electronica Solutions. The
6529 Network Museum should preserve authority and credit for each function when
adapting a lesson. Technological novelty, immersive scale, award status, or
prototype visibility should not be used as a substitute for collection
eligibility, provenance, rights, custody, or conservation evidence.
