# Centre Pompidou

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The Centre Pompidou describes a collection and research structure that joins
modern and contemporary art with film, sound, digital media, design, and
architecture. Its [organisational page](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/centre-pompidou/organisation/divisions-and-departments)
states that the National Museum of Modern Art / Industrial Design Center
inventories, conserves, restores, presents, and documents collections that
include new media. It names separate new-media and restoration departments and
identifies the Kandinsky Library as a research and documentation centre with a
reading room. These are stated institutional functions; they are not, by
themselves, proof of every conservation workflow.

The [Film and New media collection overview](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/collection/film-and-new-media)
dates this collection to 1976 and describes film, video, sound, and digital
media as emerging and ephemeral media. It states that newly acquired works are
preserved in their original format. That statement establishes institutional
intent; the *Zapping Zone* case below documents conservation research on a
named work.

The Centre's public-access system is also plural. [Pompidou+](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/pompidou)
describes more than 200,000 freely accessible digital resources across
collection records, videos, podcasts, virtual exhibitions, educational
resources, and audiovisual archives. The [research index](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/pompidou-plus/magazine/rubrique/research)
exposes language options including French, English, Spanish, Italian, Chinese,
Japanese, German, Portuguese, and Russian. Object identity is connected to
distinct research and access formats across those language routes.

## Close reading: Vera Molnar, Sans titre

The Centre's [object record for Vera Molnar's *Sans titre*](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/cxx9ErA)
identifies the work as a 1970 drawing from the cycle “A la recherche de Paul
Klee.” It records the artist, title, date, algorithmic-drawing description,
Chinese ink on paper, dimensions of 30 × 30 cm, 2002 acquisition, and inventory
number AM 2002-84. Its bibliography includes page and figure references and
links to the Bibliothèque Kandinsky catalogue.

Its structure keeps work identity, series, material description, acquisition,
inventory, and bibliography in separate fields. For a chain-native museum, the
equivalent is to keep token and
project identity, work medium, technical constitution, acquisition event, rights
status, and research references separately addressable and cross-linked.

## Conservation case: Zapping Zone

The Centre's [research and restoration page for Chris Marker's *Zapping Zone*](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/offer-to-professionals/scientific-research/zapping-zone-chris-marker)
describes a 1990 interactive installation composed of thirteen television
sets, seven Apple II GS computer stations, four luminous displays containing
eighty slides, and ten photomontages. The page documents a PATRIMA research
project with two researchers and the C2RMF, historical-documentation study,
photographic and radiographic documentation of the Apple II GS computers, and
technical service of the original equipment. It also describes planned
reinstallation and the reactivation of obsolete programs.

The page demonstrates conservation research by naming the work's components,
researchers, partner, documentary method, and technical actions. It describes
the exhibition and future public availability as planned outcomes; their
completion requires later evidence. The Museum's preservation records should
make the same temporal distinction.

The Centre's longer research writing applies the same caution to online
exhibition history. In [“Erreur 404: une histoire de l'exposition artistique
en ligne”](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/pompidou-plus/magazine/article/erreur-404-une-histoire-de-lexposition-artistique-en-ligne),
published 22 July 2025, Hugo du Plessix describes research based on eleven
interviews and more than sixteen hours of exchanges. The essay retains
funding instability, changing technical roles, obsolete tools, and criticism
of simply reproducing the white cube online. It treats institutional history
as contested infrastructure, with loss and inaccessibility left visible.

## What the Museum should adopt

- make object records resolve to bibliography, research, access, and
  preservation manifestations without merging their different purposes;
- describe digital works through components, software or hardware, duration,
  display conditions, dependencies, and technical status;
- separate completed conservation actions from planned reinstallation,
  reactivation, or public-access outcomes;
- preserve the distinction between original formats and access manifestations;
- publish the participants, methods, unresolved questions, and evidence limits
  of research projects;
- offer language and accessibility metadata for each public manifestation.

## Where the analogy ends

An object page is not a complete conservation report, and a large digital
resource count is not evidence that every resource is deeply connected to its
object. The *Zapping Zone* page documents a research and restoration project,
but its planned outputs must not be recorded as completed preservation. The
Museum should transfer the Centre's separations between identity, research,
technical evidence, and public access—not its scale or resource volume.

2. Centre Pompidou, [“Film and New media”](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/collection/film-and-new-media).
3. Centre Pompidou, [“Sans titre” — Vera Molnar](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/cxx9ErA), 1970 work date shown.

# Centro Multimedia, CENART — Research and Production Center

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

Centro Multimedia is a research, production, training, and documentation
center. No collecting remit was found in the sources reviewed. Its [Virtual
Library](https://cmm.cenart.gob.mx/acercaDe.php) gathers catalogues, essays,
exhibition booklets, augmented-reality stories, and files produced by the
Center. The library makes program history part of the public record while
leaving production support, research, and collection custody as separate
questions.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Laboratories organize a public research program

The official [Centro Multimedia profile](https://cmm.cenart.gob.mx/acercaDe.php) records a 1994 founding and seven laboratories, including sound experimentation, digital visualities, robotics and complex systems, research in arts and technologies, extended realities and videogames, and digital publications. Its programs cover training, dissemination, production support, residencies, and research and experimentation.

The structure gives a project a place in a research ecology: laboratory, program, collaborators, production stage, and public result can be recorded without claiming that every supported work entered a permanent collection.

### 2. The Virtual Library preserves publication and program memory

Centro Multimedia describes the Virtual Library as a place for analog and digital publications produced by the Center. Its holdings include catalogues, essays, exhibition booklets, augmented-reality stories, and files. The publication archive is therefore evidence of how the institution taught, exhibited, and debated electronic art in Mexico.

### 3. Audiovisual records receive a separate archive

The [Audiovisual Archive of Centro Multimedia](https://archivoaudiovisualcmm.omeka.net/) describes a database of audiovisual material produced between 1994 and 2002. Its separate interface makes event and program documentation discoverable without presenting documentation as equivalent to the works documented.

### 4. The program remains active

The Mexican government announcement [“El Centro Multimedia del CENART inicia
2026…”](https://www.gob.mx/cultura/prensa/el-centro-multimedia-del-cenart-inicia-2026-con-actividades-formativas-expositivas-y-de-exploracion-tecnologica?idiom=es-MX),
dated 13 January 2026, records continuing workshops, seminars, exhibitions,
talks, and exploration across transmedia, videogames, animation, philosophy,
digital image, and editorial practice. The dated program extends the
institutional history beyond the archive's earlier holdings.

## Publication and scholarship

Centro Multimedia's Spanish-language publication style is programmatic and archival. Laboratory work, exhibitions, seminars, residencies, and publications appear as connected forms of research. The writing lesson is to preserve the sequence from question to experiment to public artifact, while naming the institutional role at each stage.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Create project and program records distinct from accession records.
- Record laboratory, residency, collaborator, toolchain, production, publication, and exhibition relationships.
- Preserve catalogues, essays, exhibition booklets, talks, and audiovisual documentation as citable research objects.
- Provide original-language sources and identify translation status.
- State whether the Museum commissioned, produced, exhibited, documented, hosted, or acquired a work.

## Where the analogy ends

Public evidence reviewed does not establish a Centro Multimedia accession or digital-conservation policy. Its archive demonstrates research infrastructure and cultural memory, not permanent custody of every project. 6529 should adopt the lifecycle and publication logic without converting production support into accession.

# Dia Art Foundation

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

Robert Smithson's *Spiral Jetty* is published by Dia as both a collection object
and a changing site. The [collection record](https://www.diaart.org/collection/collection/smithson-robert-spiral-jetty-1970-1999-014)
identifies the work as 1970, gives its materials as black basalt rock, salt
crystals, earth, and water, records its approximate dimensions as 18,000 by 180
inches, assigns reference number 1999.014, and locates it at the Great Salt
Lake. The record keeps material identity, site, credit, and interpretive
context together without treating the site as a static image.

## A site-specific record with a longitudinal condition view

Dia's [project page for *Spiral Jetty*](https://www.diaart.org/exhibition/exhibitions-projects/robert-smithson-spiral-jetty-site/)
describes Dia's stewardship, visitor conditions, environmental change, public
partners, rights, and the work's relation to water level and entropy. It also
states that Dia has commissioned aerial documentation once or twice a year in
spring and fall since 2012. The [aerial documentation index](https://www.diaart.org/collection/spiraljettyaerials)
lists dated images through Spring 2026.

The decisive practice is serial observation. Dia does not make one undated
condition statement stand for the work's entire history; it publishes a chain
of observations tied to place and date. Its prose moves from object identity to
site, stewardship, visitor access, environmental circumstance, and repeated
documentation. That is a stronger public record for a changing work than a
single descriptive paragraph, but it remains a physical-site method.

For the 6529 Network Museum, a site-, environment-, or service-dependent work
should have separate linked records for identity, current condition,
observation method, location or runtime, access constraints, image or data
rights, responsible parties, and unresolved change. A recurring observation
should record the date, instrument or method, source file or image, operator,
conditions, and relation to the previous observation. The Museum should never
turn a later observation into an undated claim about the work's original state.

## History and publication as institutional evidence

Dia's [history page](https://www.diaart.org/about/historyofdia) uses an
interactive timeline for its fiftieth anniversary, combining archive documents,
photographs, video, ephemera, and the voices of artists, curators, and
caretakers. Dia's [publication page](https://www.diaart.org/shop/dia-publications)
describes artist monographs, exhibition and collection catalogues, artist books,
poetry, readers, and critical theory, with named editors and contributors.

The publication genre is work-centered and sustained. A collection object is
not asked to carry the entire institutional history; the object record, site
project, serial documentation, archive timeline, and longer publication each
perform a different editorial task. Dia's contact page states that its archive
is a comprehensive repository of institutional and program history undergoing
multi-year processing, preservation, and access work, and is not currently
available for research. The Museum should therefore distinguish an archive's
existence from public research access.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Use a dated observation series for changing physical or networked works.
- Separate object identity, site or runtime, stewardship, visitor access,
  condition, rights, and serial documentation.
- Publish archive timelines from named primary materials and identify the
  voices or roles represented in each historical account.
- Treat artist/work publications, collection records, and institutional history
  as linked but distinct genres.
- Mark archive processing and access status explicitly.

## Where the analogy ends

Dia's evidence concerns a land-based sculpture, environmental change, recurring
aerial photography, and a publication and archive program. It does not
demonstrate digital-art conservation, token preservation, software migration,
or chain-data governance. The Museum should adopt the dated-observation and
work-centered publication structures without importing Dia's physical-site
custodial assumptions.

# Getty

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

Getty’s public documentation is useful as a model of connected collection and
research infrastructure. The Museum Collection API describes more than
250,000 object records, including deaccessioned objects, and exposes objects,
people, groups, places, exhibitions, documents, images, and activities through
Linked Art JSON-LD, IIIF, REST, ActivityStreams, and SPARQL. The same
documentation warns that the data can be incomplete or contain errors, is
still being updated, and does not carry a guarantee of curatorial approval.
[Getty Museum Collection API Documentation](https://data.getty.edu/museum/collection/docs/)

That qualification is part of the institutional profile. Getty’s systems make
semantics, relations, identifiers, and change visible, while their own
documentation tells users where the data remains provisional. The [Getty
Vocabularies](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/index.html)
extend this approach beyond object records: they describe structured resources
with sources, contributors, historical information, variant names, complex
relationships, multilingual terms, and disputed or ambiguous art-historical
information.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Provenance has explicit notation

Getty’s [Research on Museum Collection
Provenance](https://www.getty.edu/museum/provenance/) page explains how its
public provenance format handles date ranges, “by” dates, open-ended
intervals, unknown owners, private collections, dealers, transactions, sales,
locations, and source notes. It gives distinct meanings to forms such as
`1955–1970`, `1955–`, `–1955`, and `by 1955–`; it also explains that a private
collection may identify an anonymous owner or withhold a known identity.

The lesson for a chain-native Museum is exact semantic typing. “Unknown,”
“private,” “disputed,” and “not yet researched” should not share one empty
field. A provenance interval, owner identity, transaction, and source note
should be separate assertions with their own uncertainty and revision status.

### 2. An object record joins history, scholarship, and identifiers

The Getty page for Vittore Carpaccio’s *Hunting on the Lagoon* (recto) and
*Letter Rack* (verso) provides Provenance, Bibliography, and Exhibitions as
distinct research paths. Its provenance sequence names owners and date ranges,
retains source notes, and records uncertainty such as “possibly.” The page
also exposes an API URL, TMS and DOR identifiers, a SPARQL route, a permalink,
and a “Last updated: June 2, 2026” notice for the primary JSON-LD document.
[Hunting on the Lagoon (recto); Letter Rack
(verso)](https://www.getty.edu/art/collection/object/103REK)

The record therefore documents two histories: the artwork’s reported passage
through owners and the catalogue’s own addressability and update state. For
the 6529 Network Museum, a token transfer should remain one event in a larger
provenance graph. It cannot, by itself, prove legal title, donor authority,
artist attribution, consent, or the condition of the work.

### 3. APIs expose a graph and a change vocabulary

The Museum Collection API documentation lists entity types for objects, places,
documents, groups, people, exhibitions, and activities. It describes Linked
Art JSON-LD and RDF graph queries through SPARQL, IIIF image and presentation
services, and ActivityStreams for tracking record changes. These choices make
relations and updates queryable alongside page prose.
[Getty Museum Collection API Documentation](https://data.getty.edu/museum/collection/docs/)

The 6529 Network Museum can apply this at a smaller scale by publishing typed
relations among works, wallets, artists, contracts, transactions, exhibitions,
documents, images, and conservation events. The on-chain layer should hold
authorized assertions and durable lineage; public exports should expose the
larger research graph without pretending that every assertion has the same
status.

### 4. Vocabularies carry provenance and disagreement

The Getty Vocabularies page describes its resources as more than lists of
preferred labels. Entries can connect to published sources and contributors,
other resources, historical and current information, variant names,
multilingual terms, and debated or ambiguous art-historical information. The
vocabularies are published as Linked Open Data and are intended for cataloguers,
researchers, and data providers. [Getty
Vocabularies](https://www.getty.edu/research/tools/vocabularies/index.html)

For the Museum, a term such as “interactive,” “generative,” or “software-based”
should have an identifier, definition, source, contributor, revision history,
and alternatives where relevant. A vocabulary is an evidentiary layer, not a
permanent tag embedded without explanation in an accession record.

### 5. Digital catalogues are planned as publications

The Getty Foundation’s 2017 [*Museum Catalogues in the Digital
Age*](https://www.getty.edu/publications/osci-report/) is the final report of
the Online Scholarly Catalogue Initiative. It treats the online catalogue as a
web publication with notes, media, rights, citations, multiple reading paths,
and revision. Its structure includes projects at a glance, lessons learned,
approaches, costs, remaining challenges, evaluation, functional requirements,
rights documentation, a user study, and a glossary.

The report’s public-writing value lies in its operational detail. It makes
catalogue design answerable to audiences, existing systems, rights, labour,
maintenance, and preservation. A Museum publication from GitHub or
content-addressed records should therefore have a citable edition, accessible
web reading, open formats where rights permit, stable links, and an explicit
plan for revisions and preservation.

## Close reading of public scholarship

The Carpaccio object page uses a restrained, notation-led voice. “Provenance,”
“Bibliography,” and “Exhibitions” are separate invitations to research rather
than headings inside one undifferentiated narrative. The provenance sequence
uses dates, owners, source notes, and qualified language; identifiers and an
update date tell the reader how to address the record itself. The editorial
style teaches the reader how to read the evidence by making its units visible.
[Hunting on the Lagoon (recto); Letter Rack
(verso)](https://www.getty.edu/art/collection/object/103REK)

The OSCI report uses a different but complementary voice. It is a long-form
institutional research document organized around implementation questions:
what participating institutions built, what systems and rights they needed,
how users read the results, what the work cost, and what remains difficult.
Its headings, downloadable requirements, rights form, user study, and glossary
make the report usable as a design record with testable requirements.
The page’s preservation discussion is especially relevant: a stable PDF does
not preserve interactive audio or video, and a changing online catalogue needs
planned capture and continuing maintenance. [*Museum Catalogues in the Digital
Age*](https://www.getty.edu/publications/osci-report/)

## What the Museum should adopt

- Give provenance dates, owner identities, transactions, source notes, and
  uncertainty different fields and identifiers.
- Publish an object graph with typed relations and stable cross-system IDs;
  include a machine-readable change record and a human-readable update notice.
- Treat wallet custody, token transfer, legal title, donor authority, artist
  attribution, consent, and condition as separate claims with separate
  evidence.
- Build small, versioned vocabularies whose definitions, sources, contributors,
  alternatives, and revisions are public.
- Design essays and catalogues as maintainable publications: specify citation,
  rights, accessibility, export, versioning, and preservation before release.

## Where the analogy ends

The Getty API documentation identifies the data as work in progress and warns
of incompleteness, errors, and ongoing change. The Museum should snapshot and
identify any external Getty-derived data it uses; an API response is not a
substitute for checking the underlying record or preserving the retrieval
state. Getty’s vocabulary and publication systems also reflect long-running
institutional labour. A small Museum should adopt the semantics it can govern,
not copy the full graph or vocabulary surface.

The OSCI report also sets a boundary around digital publication. A web page can
remain available while its interactive media, dependencies, or previous
versions become inaccessible. The Museum needs explicit capture, media
preservation, rights, and migration procedures. Getty’s open-data terms do not
automatically determine the rights in an artwork, an artist’s software, a
third-party text, or a hosted image.

# Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The Guggenheim’s [“The Conserving Computer-Based Art
Initiative”](https://www.guggenheim.org/conservation/the-conserving-computer-based-art-initiative)
describes an ongoing, practice-based research project on computer-based works
in the collection. The page documents a survey and backup of artist-provided
hardware and software, disk images, dependency research, source-code analysis,
artist interviews, treatment testing, and dissemination through public
presentations and publications.

## From components to significant properties

The initiative’s public workflow records hardware, operating systems,
programming languages, libraries, peripherals, media files, and relationships
among dependencies. It also publishes acquisition checklists, a component
spreadsheet, disk-imaging reports, and related documentation.

The Guggenheim describes source-code analysis as a way to document intended
behaviors and significant properties that may not be visible during a single
viewing. The page notes that computer-science collaboration is necessary for
this work because most conservators are not trained to read the relevant
programming languages.

The initiative uses Identity Reports for enduring characteristics and
Iteration Reports for a particular installation. For a chain-native work, the
6529 Network Museum should use the same record boundary: the identity record
should state what is being preserved, while each installation, migration, or
fallback should receive a dated iteration record that names the environment,
changes, tests, authority, and residual differences.

## Restoration made visible

The [*Brandon* credits and restoration
page](https://brandon.guggenheim.org/credits/) states that the 2016–17
restoration addressed Java applets that no longer displayed correctly, broken
links, incorrect typography, an inoperable Mooplay interface, and inaccessible
virtual court records. It says original code was retained and commented out
when no longer executed; additions were documented through source-code
annotation, version control, and treatment reporting. Java applets were
replaced with JavaScript functions and animated GIFs, and other obsolete web
structures were replaced with documented equivalents.

The [“About net.flag”](https://netflag.guggenheim.org/html/about.html) page
records the work’s migration from Java to JavaScript and the decisions made
around historical flag designs and countries absent from the original set.
These pages identify the intervention, the people involved, the technical
changes, and the remaining relationship to the earlier work.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Create an identity record before accession that names significant
  properties, artist or estate authority, dependencies, and rights to preserve
  source, executable, media, and environment.
- Produce a bit-for-bit preservation image where a storage device is part of
  the work, record fixity and imaging conditions, and retain the original
  environment description.
- Maintain separate iteration records for every installation, migration,
  dependency replacement, or fallback build.
- Use code review and behavioral tests to record states, randomness,
  interaction, external data, timing, and failure modes.
- Publish intervention credits, decision rationales, before-and-after
  evidence, version-control references, and treatment reports when rights
  permit.

## Where the analogy ends

The Guggenheim’s documented work relies on a CCBA fellowship, collaboration
with New York University computer science, conservation staff, artist-provided
systems, and case-specific authority. A public checklist cannot create those
relationships. Source code is one evidentiary layer; display, interaction,
sound, context, reception, rights, and artist or estate decisions must remain
separately documented. Identity and iteration reports organize judgment; they
do not decide it.

## Sources

1. Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, [“The Conserving Computer-Based Art Initiative”](https://www.guggenheim.org/conservation/the-conserving-computer-based-art-initiative).
2. Shu Lea Cheang and Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, [“Brandon: credits and restoration”](https://brandon.guggenheim.org/credits/).
3. Mark Napier and Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, [“About net.flag”](https://netflag.guggenheim.org/html/about.html).
4. Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, [“Seeing Double: Emulation in Theory and Practice”](https://www.guggenheim.org/exhibition/seeing-double-emulation-in-theory-and-practice), 2004.

# HEK Basel

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

## Institutional profile

A current page for knowbotic research's *minds of concern, New York version*
(2002) begins with a preservation fact: Flash no longer renders in current
browsers. HEK supplies a browser-emulated route for the software context of
2002, Internet Archive links for external material, and a separate
non-emulated mobile route. Popups and external links are listed as limitations.
The record therefore describes access as a dated technical condition, with no
guarantee that the route will remain permanent. [*minds of concern*](https://moc.hek.ch/)

HEK's collection page places born-digital, software, net-based, interactive,
and participatory works at the center of its remit. It describes acquisitions
from a 2010–2012 research project, donations, and permanent loans, alongside
care for digital works in the Swiss Federal Art Collection and Kunstkredit.
[Collection](https://hek.ch/en/collection/)

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Collection work starts with technical inquiry

HEK says inventory begins with technical staff and external IT or conservation
expertise. Documentation is followed by a preservation solution matched to the
work. Its public research pages link case studies on emulation, digital
archiving, and specific works. [Research and
Restauration](https://hek.ch/en/collection/research-and-restauration/)

The digital-archive study reports a collection of more than 90 works and about
150 digital archival information packages. It describes automated integrity
checks and replacement of corrupted material from correct copies. Those are
institution-reported figures and procedures; the transferable evidence is the
record structure and the explicit fixity problem. [From a manual to an
automated digital archive at HEK](https://hek.ch/en/collection/research-and-restauration/fallstudie-digitales-archiv-hek/)

### 2. Conservation reports retain the work's context

The *TraceNoizer* case study follows a web-based work made in 2001 through its
offline and online history, HEK's 2017 acquisition, and the technical and
techno-cultural context needed for presentation. It names artist interview,
web documentation, and the supplied digital archive as evidence. [Conservation
case study: TraceNoizer by LAN](https://hek.ch/en/collection/research-and-restauration/conservation-case-study-tracenoizer-by-lan/)

The *Communimage* report records a 2020 version acquired in 2023, earlier
artist updates, a 2024 local demonstration, source code stored outside the
website container, and Java/JVM dependency. Its account joins interaction,
source, installation problem, and proposed presentation state. [Communimage
case study](https://cms.hek.ch/files/downloads/CaseStudy-Communimage.pdf)

### 3. Collection records can describe generative chain-native work

HEK's *ConcretionX144X160 #3* page identifies three acquired works from a
114-part generative NFT series, the work's Game Boy-like format, four-color
palette, animation, online/NFT form, fxhash link, and the three collection
iterations. The page supplies a concrete object record while keeping the token
page from standing in for the institutional record.
[*ConcretionX144X160 #3*](https://hek.ch/en/collection/artworks/concretionx144x160-3/)

HEK also documents public software and network programs through [Projects](https://hek.ch/en/projects/),
including HEK Net Works from March 2020 and Net Encounters from January to
June 2021.

## Close reading of public scholarship

HEK's case-study prose moves in a useful order: identify the work; establish
its historical and acquisition context; describe behavior and dependencies;
name the intervention; then leave residual uncertainty visible. The writing
keeps “digital preservation” concrete. Java, Flash, source location, external
links, browser behavior, and local demonstration are the terms in which the
argument is made.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Require a work-specific technical-constitution record covering source,
  dependencies, runtime, browser, external services, hardware, chain/token,
  mutability, and display assumptions.
- Record original, current, migrated, emulated, documentary, and fallback
  states separately, with dates, evidence, responsible reviewers, and known
  losses.
- Publish conservation case studies that connect acquisition, artist input,
  technical diagnosis, intervention, current access, and remaining limits.
- Add catalogue fields for public data route, rights status, and whether the
  Museum holds source, capture, runtime, token, or only permission to link.

## Where the analogy ends

HEK has collection authority, conservation staff, and technical partnerships
that the 6529 Network Museum does not automatically possess. An NFT catalogue
entry does not establish title, custody, rights clearance, or preservation
completion. No public structured API was identified in the reviewed material.

# Laboratorio Arte Alameda — Research and Documentation Center

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

Laboratorio Arte Alameda is a research, production, exhibition, and
documentation center for art and technology. The sources reviewed do not
establish a collecting-museum remit. The INAH publication [“Conservación del
acervo documental del Laboratorio Arte
Alameda”](https://revistas.inah.gob.mx/index.php/digitales/article/view/4637),
published 5 December 2013, begins with the practical problem of accessing,
storing, disseminating, and preserving the documentary materials generated by
institutional work. That problem gives the Center's public scholarship a
precise archival subject.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Institutional role is stated precisely

The official [INBA profile](https://inba.gob.mx/recinto/32) describes LAA as a space for exhibition, documentation, production, and research in practices that put art and technology into dialogue. It identifies the Príamo Lozada Documentation Center, specialized in new-media art, and lists conferences, concerts, projections, seminars, and workshops.

The opening distinction matters. LAA's public evidence establishes a research and documentation function; it should not be described as a permanent collection simply because it presents or documents digital and electronic art.

### 2. Documentary preservation is published as a case

The INAH article [“Conservación del acervo documental del Laboratorio Arte Alameda”](https://revistas.inah.gob.mx/index.php/digitales/article/view/4637) records the need to access, store, disseminate, and preserve materials produced through daily institutional work. Its subject is the documentary archive, not a generalized promise to preserve all digital artworks.

This is a useful model for 6529: identify the material corpus, name the risk or access problem, state the preservation decision, and keep the documentary record distinct from the artwork record.

### 3. Open repositories can have editorial control

[Modos de Oír](https://modosdeoir.inba.gob.mx/) is an open digital repository developed by LAA and Ex Teresa around sound-art practices in Mexico. Its public description identifies an editorial committee and an initial group of 120 works researched for an exhibition. The repository is therefore both an access surface and an edited research project.

### 4. Documentation is supported by a specialist center and publication

The government announcement for the [Príamo Lozada Documentation Center](https://www.gob.mx/cultura/prensa/el-laboratorio-arte-alameda-inaugurara-su-centro-de-documentacion-priamo-lozada) describes books, journals, brochures, audio, video, and other documentation made available to researchers, students, and artists. The 2025 book announcement [“Prácticas artísticas, posconceptualismo electrónico y transmodernidad”](https://inba.gob.mx/prensa/22177/laboratorio-arte-alameda-presentara-el-libro-practicas-artisticas-posconceptualismo-electronico-y-transmodernidad) demonstrates a further publication form: regional art-historical research on electronic and digital practices.

## Publication and scholarship

LAA combines institutional description, a documentation center, a formal conservation study, an editorially governed repository, and regional art-historical publication. Its writing moves from documentary problem to access and preservation decision, then outward to the history of practices. The model is valuable because it does not require documentary holdings and artworks to be the same kind of record.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Create a documentary-holdings record separate from artwork accession.
- Record the source, creator, date, format, rights, condition, and access route for exhibition and program materials.
- Use editorial review and source notes for public repositories.
- Publish conservation cases around exact materials, decisions, and unresolved limitations.
- Preserve original-language bibliographies and provide clearly identified translations.

## Where the analogy ends

The INAH conservation article concerns documentary holdings, not necessarily the conservation of digital artworks. Public evidence reviewed does not establish a complete LAA accession or digital-condition schema. The Museum should adopt the Center's documentary discipline without calling documentation custody.

# Los Angeles County Museum of Art

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

LACMA’s [“Welcome to the Art + Tech
Lab”](https://www.lacma.org/lab) states that the Lab supports experiments in
design, creative entrepreneurship, art and industry, collaboration, and
interdisciplinary dialogue. The page links current projects to the original
1967–71 program catalogue and keeps a dated Lab Archive of artists and
projects.

The page’s dated record for Casey Reas’s *METAVASARELY* and *An Empty Room*,
alongside the artist interview [“Introducing METAVASARELY and An Empty Room,
A Two-Part Digital Work by Casey
Reas”](https://unframed.lacma.org/2023/02/13/introducing-metavasarely-and-empty-room-two-part-digital-work-casey-reas),
provides a named example of this continuity.

## *METAVASARELY* and the program archive

LACMA’s interview states that the project is a simulation and homage to Victor
Vasarely’s unrealized proposal for the original Art & Technology Program. The
proposal described a machine with lights arranged in a grid that would generate
millions of visual patterns related to Vasarely’s paintings. Reas explains that
he chose a software simulation in place of a physical electronic build.
For LACMA, he describes creating one work in each of two forms: *METAVASARELY*
and *An Empty Room*. The page says both have online and in-gallery components,
beginning with *METAVASARELY* on lacma.org.

This record is precise enough to separate the historical proposal, Reas’s
software simulation, the two-part project, and the current presentation. A
6529 program page should preserve the call, selection decision, artist brief,
source documents, project components, minting or accession event, exhibition
history, and later preservation status as linked records.

## Colloquium as a care record

Joey Heinen’s [“Examining the Life and Times of Media Art at LACMA’s First-Ever
Time-Based Media Colloquium”](https://unframed.lacma.org/node/3597) identifies
the event as **TBM IRL: Examining Lifecycles of Time-Based Media Art**, a
daylong colloquium held on October 27, 2023, at the Academy Museum of Motion
Pictures. The account names artists, gallerists, collectors, archivists,
estate representatives, and museum professionals as participants.

The article records questions about what defines authenticity across time,
who is authorized to make preservation decisions, whether artist intent is the
controlling rule, how an ideal state relates to technological change, and how
to steward works that depend on obsolescent technologies. It also identifies
artist archives, authorship and authority, AI, blockchain, and big data as
topics. The author’s stated takeaway is advocacy for the resources and labor
required to care for time-based media.

For each time-based or network-dependent work, the Museum should turn those
questions into required record fields: work definition; authorized decision
makers; acceptable change; period-specific and current environments;
accessibility and embodiment needs; dependencies; recurring labor and budget;
test evidence; and unresolved questions.

## Blockchain acquisition: ambition and evidence

LACMA’s [“LACMA Acquires Largest Collection of Blockchain
Artworks”](https://www.lacma.org/press/lacma-acquires-largest-collection-blockchain-artworks),
dated February 13, 2023, states that a gift from Cozomo de’ Medici placed 22
digital artworks by 13 artists in or promised to the permanent collection. The
release quotes LACMA’s director describing the acquisition as an impetus to
develop new standards and techniques for preserving works created on the
blockchain.

That preservation language is a stated institutional ambition. The release
documents an acquisition; it supplies no public schema or condition model. The 6529
Network Museum should publish the next layer as linked, testable documentation:
chain and token identifiers; custody and provenance events; artist, collector,
and museum rights; source and dependency inventory; display and access
requirements; condition tests; preservation decisions; and named responsible
roles.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Keep program history, artist/work records, acquisitions, exhibitions, and
  preservation builds as distinct linked events.
- Use a work-level authority and authenticity record for media works, with
  explicit rules for reinstallation, migration, and acceptable change.
- Budget recurring technical labor and record who is responsible for each
  dependency, service, and preservation test.
- Convene artists, conservators, curators, registrars, archivists, technicians,
  and rights staff around a named work and publish the resulting decisions.
- Treat blockchain preservation standards as versioned public specifications
  tested against named collection works.

## Where the analogy ends

LACMA’s Art + Tech pages combine program description, archive links, project
pages, interviews, and acquisition announcements. Those forms serve different
editorial purposes and should not be treated as one collection-data model. The
blockchain release documents the acquisition and the intention to develop
preservation standards; it does not, by itself, demonstrate a completed
technical or provenance method.

2. Joel Ferree, [“Introducing METAVASARELY and An Empty Room, A Two-Part Digital Work by Casey Reas”](https://unframed.lacma.org/2023/02/13/introducing-metavasarely-and-empty-room-two-part-digital-work-casey-reas), LACMA, 13 February 2023.

# LI-MA

## Institutional profile

LI-MA's ArtHost research starts from the practical failure of treating a net-art
URL as a preservation package. The proposed service receives documentation,
source, and domain information from an artist or collection; checks the work
and its dependencies; and gives the work a per-work virtual machine. The
architecture hosts the work while retaining the materials needed to understand
how it operates. [ArtHost research](https://li-ma.nl/article/arthost-research/)

This makes LI-MA relevant to 6529 as preservation infrastructure. Its public
site joins preservation, research, knowledge resources, projects, and
collection services; its ownership model is a separate question.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Preservation is a sequence of distinct operations

LI-MA's introduction to digital-art preservation distinguishes storage,
migration, digitisation, emulation, virtualization, documentation, and
reinterpretation. Migration changes source material for a new platform;
emulation preserves an earlier environment without changing the source. The
page also describes source-code storage and artist input. [What Are the Basics
of Preserving Digital Art?](https://li-ma.nl/article/preservation-introduction/)

Its storage page describes a repository for media art and an ArtHost workflow
that inventories the work, checks dependencies, transfers a domain where
needed, stores source and documentation, and provides a virtual server.
[Storage](https://li-ma.nl/article/storage/)

### 2. Documentation carries its own status

LI-MA's documentation service records content, historical context, technical
specification, configurations, installation, acquisition and exhibition
history, condition, versions, iterations, and preservation actions. It uses
text, video, screenshots, manuals, MediaWiki case studies, and GitLab version
control. [The importance of documentation in art preservation](https://li-ma.nl/article/documentation)

The Artwork Documentation Tool then draws a clear boundary around artist
intake. Its eight steps cover working notes, backups, software, hardware,
playback, wiring, key information, video registration, and additional material;
the tool states that its data is not itself stored or preserved for the future.
[Artwork Documentation Tool](https://li-ma.nl/article/artwork-documentation-tool/)

### 3. Research is fed back into collection workflows

The Collaborative Infrastructure for Digital Art project involved 15
participating collections, 10 artists, advising parties, case studies,
training, and public dissemination. LI-MA reports implementation of results in
workflow, metadata, storage, and monitoring. Its UNFOLD program treats
reinterpretation as a collaborative response to new technology, context, and
audience. [Collaborative Infrastructure for Digital Art](https://li-ma.nl/article/collaborative-infrastructure-for-digital-art/)
· [UNFOLD](https://li-ma.nl/article/unfold/)

## Close reading of public scholarship

LI-MA publishes knowledge as a set of usable forms: a preservation primer, a
case-study page, a documentation tool, a storage description, a research
report, and symposium records. The ArtHost cases name the work-specific
problem—third-party influence in *Chinese Gold*, identity and participation in
*Mouchette.org*—before describing infrastructure. This keeps technology
subordinate to the work's behavior, context, and preservation decision.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Split the Museum record into intake documentation, preservation package,
  technical constitution, monitoring, intervention history, and reinterpretation.
- At accession, collect artist instructions, source, dependencies, runtime,
  domain/service assumptions, installation behavior, and an evidence package.
- Mark documentation, storage, migration, emulation, virtualization, and
  reinterpretation as distinct actions with dates and responsible parties.
- Give each action a public summary and a restricted technical annex where
  source, rights, security, or credentials require limits.
- Use artist-facing forms as intake instruments only; route their data into a
  controlled, versioned Museum record.

## Where the analogy ends

LI-MA's institutional role is preservation and service; title-holding is
outside the evidence reviewed. Its public references to NFTs show an area in
which practice is being developed. That evidence does not establish that
every NFT has been preserved.
The Museum must also determine its own custody, rights, funding, hosting, and
long-term maintenance responsibilities. No public API was identified.

# M+ — Collecting Digital and Moving-Image Culture

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

M+ is a collecting museum whose [M+ Collection](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/about-the-collection/m-collection/) includes moving image, digital installations, video games, software, and web-based works. Its public record is strongest where it keeps an artwork, an archive, a library, a conservation activity, and an access condition distinct while allowing them to be researched together.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Digital work is part of an interdisciplinary collection

The M+ Collection page places digital and moving-image work within a collection organized across design, visual art, architecture, and moving image. The broader [About the Collection](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/about-the-collection/) page separately identifies the M+ Collection, M+ Sigg, Library Special Collection, and Collection Archives. It also describes specialist conservators, research and analysis, treatment documentation, installation art, time-based media, and physical and digital access.

The separation matters for 6529. An archival document, a work, an installation instruction, and a public capture may be related without being interchangeable.

### 2. Collection management roles are named

The [M+ Collections Management Policy 2025](https://webmedia.mplus.org.hk/documents/collections_management_policy_2025_en.pdf) maps registration, records management, rights and reproductions, conservation, exhibition management, installation, and archives across the Collection & Exhibition Department. The policy makes the institutional route legible before a reader reaches an individual object.

### 3. Archives are research material, not decorative background

The magazine article [“An Introduction to the M+ Collection Archives”](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/magazine/an-introduction-to-the-m-collection-archives/) (22 March 2018) describes archival appraisal, preservation, cataloguing, research use, exhibitions, and Study Centre access. It treats archival fonds as material that can generate publications and exhibitions, while retaining archival description as a separate professional task.

### 4. Public access has rights boundaries

The [Research Centre Guidelines](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/research-centre/research-centre-guidelines/)
state that collection-archive and library material may require permission from
M+ and rights holders before publication. The
[Mediatheque](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/mediatheque/) provides mediated
moving-image access through playlists, filtering, and an Interactive Media
Room. It does not offer every item as an unrestricted download.

## Publication and scholarship

M+ publishes in layers: collection pages establish identity and scope; archive essays explain practice; policy pages expose institutional roles; research guidelines state access conditions; and the Mediatheque shapes encounter. The writing is operational and contextual. It does not require a single page to perform cataloguing, conservation, rights, and interpretation at once.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Create separate relationships for artwork, collection archive, library, related material, documentation, and display.
- Record rights and access at work or material level, including on-site, restricted, licensed, unavailable, and online states.
- Link technical-care notes to the exact work. A general policy supplies
  context, not work-level evidence.
- Preserve the distinction between an institution's collection, its research holdings, and its public interface.
- Provide regional-language source paths and identify the author and status of
  every translation.

## Where the analogy ends

M+'s policy demonstrates roles and intended practice; it does not establish a public conservation case for every digital work. Its scale, building, specialist staff, and rights relationships are not transferable assumptions. The Museum should adopt the record architecture and access honesty, not imply equivalent capacity.

## Sources

2. M+, [“About the Collection”](https://www.mplus.org.hk/en/about-the-collection/). Publication date not shown. Accessed 2026-08-04. Supports: collection, archive, library, conservation, research, treatment, and access distinctions.

# Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

MCA Chicago separates a concise collection label from the larger publication
that supplies research and interpretation. The [Collection Explorer](https://mcachicago.org/art-artists/collection/)
and a representative object page for William J. O'Brien's [*Cinaedus Table
MDCCLXXV*](https://mcachicago.org/art-artists/collection/cinaedus-table-mdcclxxv/)
use standardized fields for title, artist, date, medium, dimensions, credit,
tags, and related works. The object page is an identity and discovery record;
it does not attempt to carry a full essay or conservation dossier.

## I Was Raised on the Internet: publication as a maintained resource

MCA's [*I Was Raised on the Internet* website](https://mcachicago.org/publications/websites/i-was-raised-on-the-internet)
(2018) carries the interpretive and technical burden that the short object
record does not. It presents online-only works and readings, explains that the
works use different platforms, names production, design, editorial, curatorial,
rights, and image staff, and warns that volatile internet links may disappear.
It invites reports of missing content and identifies the site as an enduring
resource for visitors and researchers.

The exhibition page organizes approximately one hundred works from 1998 onward
into named sections and directs visitors to the exhibition website for online
works: [*I Was Raised on the Internet* exhibition](https://mcachicago.org/Exhibitions/2018/I-Was-Raised-On-The-Internet).
MCA's [websites page](https://mcachicago.org/publications/websites) describes
exhibition microsites as resources containing reading lists, playlists,
installation views, images, videos, gallery guides, reviews, and knowledge
created through research.

The decisive editorial practice is separation of genres. A label fixes identity
and discovery. A microsite gathers a research argument, works, context, credits,
rights, and public access. A book can preserve a further scholarly record. MCA's
[books catalogue](https://mcachicago.org/publications/books) includes *I Was
Raised on the Internet* among the publications that extend its exhibitions and
collection through sustained scholarship.

For the 6529 Network Museum, every public microsite or digital publication
should carry its own publication record: title, publication date, research
cutoff, scope, contributors, production system or CMS when relevant, rights,
current status, known missing content, volatile links, archive or snapshot
route, and suggested citation. The collection record should link to that
publication and leave the publication's argument intact. A correction or
missing-content report should produce a dated revision entry.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Keep object identity, interpretive essay, exhibition microsite, book, and
  technical record as distinct linked publications.
- Treat credits, rights, production roles, and source lists as part of the
  publication's evidence.
- Record link status, missing content, archive scope, current availability, and
  known differences from the original publication.
- Add a stable citation and revision history to every public web publication.
- Use short collection records to state facts, not to imply that a linked essay
  or microsite has preserved the work's runtime behavior.

## Where the analogy ends

The public MCA pages reviewed demonstrate collection-label and digital-
publication practice. They do not present a dedicated conservation dossier or
evidence of a complete digital-preservation workflow. The warning that links may
disappear is an access limitation, not proof of successful preservation. The
Museum should adopt MCA's genre separation, credits, link-status disclosure,
and correction route while keeping the limits of that evidence clear.

# The Metropolitan Museum of Art

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.1
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The Met’s public scholarship connects a collection record to several distinct
forms of evidence. The current record for Albrecht Dürer’s *Salvator Mundi*
contains an overview, catalogue entry, technical notes, provenance, exhibition
history, references, and loan restrictions, alongside structured object fields,
audio, related works, and links to the Met’s Open Access resources. [Salvator
Mundi](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436243) The design keeps
interpretation, material study, ownership history,
and reuse information addressable as separate layers under one object
number.

The same institution publishes research at longer scales. The [Heilbrunn
Timeline of Art History](https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/timeline-of-art-history)
describes itself as an expert-authored digital publication and research tool;
the current page reports more than 1,000 essays and 300 chronologies, with
regular updating and enrichment. [MetPublications](https://www.metmuseum.org/met-publications)
provides access to more than 1,700 titles from the past six decades. The
[Open Access dataset](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess) makes collection
data available for reuse, giving the public record a machine-readable path in
addition to its web presentation.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. A single object page carries typed evidence

The *Salvator Mundi* record gives each type of evidence a named section. Its
overview identifies the work as a ca. 1505 oil painting on linden by Albrecht Dürer,
gives the object number and credit line, and then separates catalogue,
technical, provenance, exhibition, reference, and loan information into named
sections. The page also identifies the work as unfinished and explains that
preparatory drawing remains visible in the face and hands. [Salvator
Mundi](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436243)

The 6529 Network Museum should use typed separation:
an object description, runtime or technical account, provenance assertion,
exhibition event, rights statement, and conservation event should be distinct
records or fields with stable links to the same Museum identifier.

### 2. Artist instruction is cited inside interpretation

Adrian Piper’s *Everything #4* is documented as edition 6/8, with a 2004 date,
dimensions, acquisition credit, and object number. Its overview explains the
work’s serial structure and records that six editions were installed in the
Met’s *Afterlives: Contemporary Art in the Byzantine Crypt* exhibition from
January 29, 2024, through January 25, 2026, to realize the artist’s preferred
dispersed mode. A numbered note identifies the supporting Met publication.
[Everything #4](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/900397)

The record links an artist’s stated preference, a curatorial decision, and a
specific installation
event. A chain-native record should similarly distinguish artist instruction,
Museum interpretation, display state, and the evidence for each.

### 3. Conservation writing publishes method and uncertainty

The Met’s 20 June 2019 essay [“After Three Hundred Years of Fading, a Dutch
Masterpiece Is Digitally Restored”](https://www.metmuseum.org/perspectives/margareta-haverman-vase-of-flowers-digital-conservation)
uses Margareta Haverman’s *A Vase of Flowers* to explain a digital
reconstruction. The account moves from pigment analysis to scanning electron
microscopy, X-ray fluorescence mapping, microscope examination, and image
adjustment. It states that the result is a close approximation of a possible
earlier appearance, not a recovered original. The essay also acknowledges that
technical equipment cannot answer every question and that some adjustments
remain judgments.

The case supplies a public model for software and generative art conservation.
A capture, emulation, or reconstructed runtime should record the observed state,
method, tools, assumptions, changes made during reconstruction, and residual
uncertainty. The record should preserve the distinction between evidence and
interpretation.

### 4. Research is connected across web publication and data

The Timeline’s essays and chronologies provide a research layer around
collection objects, while MetPublications provides a publication layer with
titles and related research paths. The Met’s Open Access repository supplies a
data path for independent use. [Heilbrunn Timeline of Art
History](https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/timeline-of-art-history),
[MetPublications](https://www.metmuseum.org/met-publications), and [Open Access
dataset](https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess)

The Museum should reproduce the connection at a scale it can sustain: every public
record should expose a stable object identifier, a readable interpretation, a
machine-readable representation, and links to the essays, exhibitions,
technical studies, and versions that materially change its meaning.

## Close reading of public scholarship

The *Salvator Mundi* page assigns different evidence to separate layers.
The overview gives a short account of the work’s status and visual evidence;
the catalogue entry and technical notes can carry specialist claims; the
provenance, exhibition history, references, and loan restrictions identify
different documentary functions. The editorial voice is compact and
descriptive. It names what the page can establish and routes the reader to the
appropriate section instead of converting every type of evidence into
continuous narrative. [Salvator
Mundi](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436243)

The Haverman essay uses a different register. It is chronological and
procedural: the reader follows the problem of fading, the examinations, the
image work, and the qualified reconstruction. The essay makes specialist
methods legible without presenting them as self-sufficient proof. Its explicit
separation of technical observation, editorial adjustment, and approximation
is the most relevant writing lesson for a Museum that will publish software
studies, render captures, and emulation reports. [“After Three Hundred Years of
Fading, a Dutch Masterpiece Is Digitally
Restored”](https://www.metmuseum.org/perspectives/margareta-haverman-vase-of-flowers-digital-conservation)

## What the Museum should adopt

- Give each work one stable Museum identifier and expose separate, typed paths
  for description, provenance, rights, display, technical study, and
  conservation.
- Put artist instructions and display decisions beside the event and source
  that support them; do not encode interpretation as custody or provenance.
- Publish conservation as a reproducible account of observations, tools,
  transformations, and uncertainty. Label reconstructions as reconstructions.
- Connect readable essays and exhibition histories to the same object record as
  the machine-readable export.
- Make correction routes and update dates visible so that a record can change
  without erasing its earlier assertions.

## Where the analogy ends

The Met’s object-page pattern depends on curatorial, conservation, library,
publishing, and data capacity that the 6529 Network Museum does not yet have.
The Museum should begin with a small set of complete, well-sourced record types.
Open data also needs an explicit
scope, snapshot, and completeness statement; reuse access does not make an
object record complete or every image freely reusable. Finally, a digital
reconstruction can document an argument without resolving the historical
uncertainty that motivated it.

# The Museum of Modern Art

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

MoMA's public collection work makes the condition of a record visible. The
Museum states that its evolving collection contains almost 200,000 works and
that the website presents more than 83,000 artworks by more than 26,000 artists.
The same collection page calls the website a work in progress, identifies
incomplete records that have not necessarily received curatorial approval, and
provides a correction route. ([About the Collection](https://www.moma.org/collection/about/))

That combination is useful for a chain-native museum because identity,
availability, approval, and completeness remain separate properties. MoMA's
collection spans objects, events, installations, film, media, and performance;
its public records therefore have to connect artwork identity with duration,
display, technical process, and exhibition history. ([Media and Performance](https://www.moma.org/about/curatorial-departments/media-performance))

## A work record with technical identity

The collection record for Refik Anadol's *Unsupervised — Machine Hallucinations
— MoMA* identifies the work as 2021–2023, gives the medium as custom hardware
and software with color, sound, and a generative algorithm using artificial
intelligence, records variable dimensions, credit, object number 757.2022, and
places it in Media and Performance. It links the record to interpretive
articles and videos, states that the record is a work in progress, and provides
a feedback route. ([Refik Anadol, *Unsupervised — Machine Hallucinations — MoMA*](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/442077))

The page shows how a work record can state technical constitution before a
longer interpretation begins. For a live or generative work, the record should
also identify which captures are documentation and which are manifestations.
The 6529 Network Museum should preserve that distinction for token, project,
runtime, display, and conservation states.

## Exhibition history with published gaps

MoMA reports more than 3,500 exhibitions since 1929. Its exhibition-history
pages can include participating artists, installation views, annotated
checklists, press releases, catalogues, subsites, videos, and essays. The
Museum also says that the materials vary by page, that the archive is a living
resource, and that important film, performance, and MoMA PS1 histories remain
in future phases or outside the current online coverage. The underlying
1929–1989 exhibition data is available for research. ([About our exhibition history](https://www.moma.org/calendar/about/exhibition-history))

The operational lesson is to model exhibition history as a set of dated
relations, each with its own evidence and completeness state. An exhibition
record should link exact object identifiers, participating artists, documents,
installation views, and catalogue resources. A missing checklist should remain
missing; it should not be inferred from the exhibition title.

## Public data and its boundaries

MoMA publishes collection and artist metadata through its official GitHub
repository. The repository documents CC0 data, citation and attribution
expectations, incomplete records, rules for identifying modified derivative
datasets, and a correction route through the collection team. It also explains
that the data is generated from an internal database and is not maintained
through public pull requests. ([MoMA collection data](https://github.com/MuseumofModernArt/collection))

MoMA's API page describes a REST service for art, exhibition, artist, and image
data, but says that external access is currently limited to MoMA staff and
partners. The public open-data repository is therefore a different publication
layer, with metadata available for reuse and image rights handled separately.
([MoMA API](https://api.moma.org/))

The 6529 Network Museum should publish stable identifiers, authority and
approval states, completeness notes, correction routes, citation instructions,
and derivative-data disclosures. It should also state whether an API is public,
restricted, or versioned for partners. A public export should not imply that
every field is final or that every associated media file is reusable.

## Media conservation as shared practice

MoMA's Media and Performance department states that it collects, exhibits, and
preserves time-based art. Its remit includes securing equipment, updating
exhibition technology, and recreating presentations whose meaning depends on
duration. ([Media and Performance](https://www.moma.org/about/curatorial-departments/media-performance))

Through *Matters in Media Art*, MoMA, SFMOMA, Tate, and the New Art Trust
published guidance for acquiring, lending, installing, and caring for video,
film, audio, and computer-based installations. The project treats care as a
shared practice among artists, lenders, registrars, technicians, conservators,
and exhibition sites. ([Matters in Media Art](https://www.moma.org/research/conservation/matters-in-media-art))

MoMA's public conservation writing describes two complementary records. The
media-conservator account emphasizes artist consultation, equipment, duration,
installation guidance, and documentation. Its technical-history case records
the device model and serial number, settings, and migration sequence used to
create later copies, with structured process-history data intended to remain
searchable. ([What Does a Media Conservator Do?](https://www.moma.org/explore/inside_out/2015/03/24/what-does-a-media-conservator-do/); [Preserving the Technical History of Media Works](https://www.moma.org/explore/inside_out/2015/05/20/preserving-the-technical-history-of-media-works/))

For a chain-native work, the corresponding record should capture contract and
token identity, source and metadata versions, dependencies, runtime, browser or
renderer behavior, display conditions, artist-approved changes, migration
authority, and the evidence for each preserved state. Token ownership fixes one
provenance layer. Technical history belongs in the linked record set.

## Public scholarship and writing method

The sampled MoMA pages use distinct publication layers. The Anadol page is a
compact object record with a controlled technical description, credit, object
number, department, related interpretation, work-in-progress notice, and
feedback route. The conservation essays then explain a technical problem in
plain language, name the people and systems involved, and describe the
consequences for future display. This division lets the object page remain
readable while giving researchers a route into process history.

## What the Museum should adopt

The 6529 Network Museum should use the same separation:

- a concise object record for identity, status, credit, and rights;
- a curatorial entry for close looking and historical argument;
- a technical record for runtime, dependencies, captures, and interventions;
- provenance, condition, preservation, and correction records with their own
  sources and revision histories.

## Where the analogy ends

MoMA's collection scale, archives, departments, and conservation resources
exceed the Museum's present scale. Its open data is metadata, not a
complete public image repository; its API is not currently an open public
service; and its historical conservation essays describe particular workflows,
not a guarantee that every media work has the same documentation depth.

The 6529 Network Museum should adopt the record states, process-history model,
and correction discipline. It should not infer preservation completeness from a
public catalogue entry or treat a reusable dataset as proof of rights to every
associated image or software dependency.

# Nam June Paik Art Center — Collection, Archive, and Media-Art Scholarship

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The Nam June Paik Art Center is a collecting museum and research archive. Its [NJP Reader #13 — *Nam June Paik's Transmission: journey over two centuries*](https://njpart.ggcf.kr/books/51), published 30 April 2024, places acquisition, exhibition, documentation, preservation, authenticity, and change around a specific media-installation problem. The Center's public scholarship is most useful when the work, its source materials, and the history of their handling remain separate records.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Collection and archive are different institutional objects

The [Collection](https://njpart.ggcf.kr/collections) includes works by Nam June Paik, related artists, and contemporary media artists, with searchable categories for video, laser, robot, television, performance, and other media. The [Archives](https://njpart.ggcf.kr/pages/archive) separate the Nam June Paik Archive, Video Archive, Studio Archive, and Museum Archive. The structure distinguishes an artwork from the records that establish its history.

### 2. The Video Archive records carriers and source relationships

The [Video Archive](https://njpart.ggcf.kr/pages/videoarchive) records 2,285 analogue tapes acquired directly from Paik in 2003. It identifies Open-Reel, U-matic, Video 8, Betacam SP, and other formats, and distinguishes editions, installation sources, performance documentation, collaborative works, and other footage. The Center also describes videotape analysis of edits and sequences.

For 6529, this is a model for recording a work's source, edition, manifestation, documentation, and carrier without treating a single file or capture as the whole work.

### 3. Oral history becomes a publication method

The [Interview Project](https://njpart.ggcf.kr/pages/interview) records interviews with Paik's colleagues and friends and publishes monograph series and interview scripts. Oral history is not presented as an unqualified substitute for object evidence; it is a named source class that can be compared with collection, studio, and exhibition records.

### 4. Readers address specific preservation questions

NJP Reader #13 addresses outdoor media installations, acquisition,
presentation, documentation, preservation, and the relation between
authenticity and change. Earlier, [NJP Reader #1 — *Contributions to an
Artistic Anthropology*](https://njpart.ggcf.kr/books/31), published 18 December
2009, extended exhibition and research through a dedicated scholarly
publication.

## Publication and scholarship

The Center combines finding aids, format inventories, oral histories, exhibition histories, and authored scholarly readers. Each form carries a different evidentiary task. The result is a publication system in which technical media analysis can sit beside historical and theoretical writing without losing the identity of the source material.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Separate artwork, edition, source, installation, performance, documentation, and carrier records.
- Record format, physical support, source relationship, and digitization or analysis event.
- Treat artist and collaborator interviews as identified evidence with date and role.
- Publish conservation essays around exact works and decisions about authenticity, change, and reconstruction.
- State whether research access is on-site, appointment-only, digitally available, restricted, or temporarily unavailable.

## Where the analogy ends

The Center's archive is materially specific to Paik's estate, studio, and analogue media. It cannot be mapped directly onto token, contract, custody, or wallet facts. Archive presence and research access do not establish title or accession.
