# NTT InterCommunication Center [ICC] — Media-Art Collection and Archive

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

ICC is a media-art collection and research center. Its 2025 case [*Restoring
Media Art Works: A Case Study of “World, Membrane and the Dismembered
Body”*](https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/archive/works/restoring-media-art-works-a-case-study-of-world-membrane-and-the-dismembered-body/)
links a collection work to investigation, restoration, re-creation, and
exhibition. ICC publishes the restoration as a work-specific event, with the
collection and exhibition histories attached.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Collection policy is tied to communication media

ICC's [Collection](https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/about/collection/) describes
works concerned with communication media and states the aim of preserving
them. Media technology enters the collection remit and the description of the
work itself.

### 2. HIVE preserves institutional program history

[About HIVE](https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/hive/about/) records exhibitions, symposia, artist talks, live events, workshops, and interviews from 1997 onward. The archive began on site in 2004 and moved onto the web in 2006. It also distinguishes licensing conditions: some videos are available under Creative Commons terms, while other materials remain subject to different access conditions.

The [HIVE archive](https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/hive/) therefore records public research and encounter without claiming that documentation is identical to the artwork.

### 3. Education and research are archived as future evidence

ICC's [Educational Activities](https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/about/education/)
connects gallery tours, workshops, seminars, artists, researchers,
universities, and external organizations to public documentation. The archive
keeps that research available after the event.

### 4. Publication connects theory and technical practice

The [*InterCommunication*](https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/about/publication/inter-communication/) journal archive spans 1992–2008 and addresses art, science, media technology, architecture, philosophy, and social questions. Alongside that theoretical publication, ICC maintains object and restoration records. The two registers can be read together without reducing a conservation decision to a general technology essay.

## Publication and scholarship

ICC's publication style moves among collection records, long-running event documentation, theoretical journals, and work-specific restoration. Dates, speakers, events, licenses, and exhibitions create a traceable institutional memory. The writing lesson is to connect a technical case to the program and collection histories that make the case intelligible.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Link collection works to exhibitions, commissions, talks, documentation, and restoration events.
- Preserve event video, transcript, speaker, date, and reuse-rights fields.
- Distinguish documentation licenses from rights in the underlying artwork.
- Publish restoration or re-enactment as a dated record with evidence, decision, intervention, and remaining difference.
- Keep a public archive of Museum research that can be cited independently of the live event.

## Where the analogy ends

ICC's NTT operating structure, physical gallery, and Japanese-language archive are institution-specific. HIVE documentation is not the artwork itself, and a license for a recorded event does not determine rights in the work discussed.

# Rhizome and the New Museum

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.1.1
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

## Institutional profile

Rhizome describes itself on its current home page as an online new-media-art
organization operating since 1996. The public site places artworks,
preservation, commissions, editorial work, and public programs in the same
web-facing program structure. Its current [ArtBase account of its own
history](https://artbase.rhizome.org/wiki/About) describes an archive of more
than 2,200 works, including websites, software, games, code, moving images,
and browsers.

Rhizome's relationship with the New Museum needs a specific description. A
2003 announcement retained in [Rhizome's own
archive](https://archive.rhizome.org/digest/?msg=00082) said that Rhizome would
operate as an affiliate, continue its programs under its own mission and core
principles, and remain a separate organizational entity while receiving office
space and administrative support from the New Museum. That is an affiliation,
not evidence that Rhizome is a New Museum department or a general governance
model for other museums.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Commissioning and selection are native to the networked program

Rhizome's current [FAQ](https://rhizome.org/FAQ/) states that commissions,
online exhibitions, ArtBase accessions, and other programs are awarded through
curatorial selection and open calls. The [current site](https://rhizome.org/)
then presents commissions, preservation, artworks, editorial work, and public
programs as navigable parts of the same public service. An online commission
can begin as a program record, a public work page, and an archival candidate.

### 2. ArtBase records the access problem instead of hiding it

The [ArtBase About page](https://artbase.rhizome.org/wiki/About) explains that
early accessions sometimes consisted of links whose targets remained outside
Rhizome's custody. When links became unstable, Rhizome stopped treating a link
as a sufficient accession. The same page distinguishes open submission,
filtered submission, and invitation-based phases; describes the 2021 relaunch
with Linked Open Data and added preservation metadata; and identifies
Webrecorder, Emulation as a Service, Conifer, and Wikibase as parts of the
technical and descriptive work.

The institutional record demonstrates stewardship by naming the failure mode,
the policy changes, and the current system. An artist's URL, a cloned capture,
an emulated environment, and Rhizome's descriptive record remain distinct.

### 3. Preservation research is published alongside the preservation tools

In [“The Making of Net Art Anthology: New from Rhizome and Google Arts &
Culture”](https://old.rhizome.org/editorial/2019/jan/28/the-making-of-net-art-anthology-rhizome-and-google-arts-culture/)
(28 January 2019), Rhizome describes the one-hundred-work Anthology through
the people and systems that made it possible: Dragan Espenschied, Lyndsey Jane
Moulds, Webrecorder, Emulation as a Service, Wikibase, a preservation matrix,
and the public exhibition. The article treats restoration, emulation,
research, exhibition, and publication as one project. Its public preservation
matrix gives each work a status and notes, leaving “archived” as a condition
that still requires explanation.

The article is a historical account of a 2019 project, not a guarantee that
every tool or service remains unchanged. Its demonstrated method is specific:
publish the access route, the preservation decision, and the
toolchain together.

### 4. A hosted-service exit is documented as an operational and access event

Rhizome announced in [“Conifer Twilight Announcement”](https://blog.conifer.rhizome.org/2025/12/15/twilight-announcement.html)
(15 December 2025) that the hosted capture-and-editing service would be
discontinued in June 2026. Its [6 May 2026 process
notice](https://blog.conifer.rhizome.org/2026/05/06/twilight-webinar.html) records
that new accounts and subscriptions had closed in December 2025 and that paid
subscriptions stopped in May 2026. At that date, replacement of the platform
with a read-only “tombstone” application remained scheduled for June. The [22 May webinar
recap](https://blog.conifer.rhizome.org/2026/05/22/webinar-recap.html) describes a
beta tombstone app, default access to existing collections, WACZ export,
Browsertrix transfer, self-hosting, redirects, and deletion. It also names
losses caused by the replayweb.page transition, including full-text search,
multiple bookmark lists, and legacy remote browsers.

The current [Conifer landing page](https://conifer.rhizome.org/) says that
creating and modifying collections was disabled before the service's June 2026
discontinuation. These public sources establish the hosted-service exit and
the available migration paths; they do not establish that every collection
has migrated successfully or that every replay is behaviorally identical.

## Close reading of public scholarship

The ArtBase page for [*My Boyfriend Came Back From the War*](https://artbase.rhizome.org/wiki/Q3933)
uses an unusually useful three-part structure. It first describes the work's
operation: nested browser frames divide into smaller frames as the visitor
clicks, producing a changing mosaic. It then separates variants and access
routes: an outside link, a cloned version with a last-known capture date, and
an emulated environment with its own date and association. Finally, it keeps
artist attribution, descriptive tags, and preservation metadata visible as
different kinds of information. The prose is compact and operational. Browser
behavior is described as behavior; the emulation and original external link
retain separate identities.

The longer [*Making of Net Art Anthology* essay](https://old.rhizome.org/editorial/2019/jan/28/the-making-of-net-art-anthology-rhizome-and-google-arts-culture/)
has a different voice: first-person institutional narration, named staff and
partners, and a sequence that moves from the Anthology's closing moment to
the practical work of research, emulation, and publication. Its exact passages
name tools and decisions. It also carries the promotional and time-bound frame
of a 2019
partnership announcement. Read with the current ArtBase and Conifer records,
it is a documented project history whose tools and service
assumptions require current verification.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Give each network-native commission a public work page, an exact creator and collaborator record, a current access route, and a separate account of external links, captures, emulations, and dependencies.
- Treat accession as a decision about custody and reproducible access, not as the discovery of a URL. Record whether the Museum holds the file, a capture, a runtime, a token, or only a permission to link.
- Publish preservation state work by work. A status matrix, retained capture package, method note, and runnable toolchain are more useful than an undated “archived” label.
- Make hosted-service dependency visible at intake. For each work, record export formats, replay software, redirects, private/public state, migration options, known feature loss, and who is responsible when the service changes.
- Keep the chain record, rights record, technical constitution, and public interpretation linked but distinct. Rhizome's ArtBase history shows why access, description, and custody cannot be inferred from one another.

## Where the analogy ends

- ArtBase is a long-accumulated archive with more than 2,200 works, changing accession policies, and uneven historical documentation. A new museum cannot reproduce that history by copying its labels or adopting its tools.
- Webrecorder, Conifer, EaaS, Wikibase, WACZ, and open-source software still require maintainers, hosting, rights permissions, version control, and migration labor. “Open source” is not a preservation outcome.
- The Conifer transition is evidence that a public hosted service can end while collections remain technically accessible through a new replay layer. It is not evidence that all future migrations will be complete, lossless, or free of new dependencies.
- The New Museum affiliation supplies a particular administrative and exhibition context. It is not a general model for legal structure, governance, or institutional autonomy.
- The 2019 Anthology essay documents a completed project and its stated preservation approach. It should not be used as current evidence for service availability, current staffing, or current access without a live check.

# Serpentine Arts Technologies

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.1.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

## Institutional profile

Serpentine Arts Technologies is presented by Serpentine Galleries as a
programme combining artist commissions, creative R&D, and strategy. Its
official [Blockchain programme page](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/arts-technologies/blockchain/)
places the Legal Lab within that programme and describes the lab as an online
research project, running from September 2019 onward, on how law can support
collaborations across art, science, and technology. Serpentine's [Future Art
Ecosystems page](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/future-art-ecosystems/)
describes FAE as an annual strategic briefing. These pages establish a
programme of commissioning, inquiry, and public strategy inside Serpentine
Galleries; they do not establish a separate museum or a collection-preservation
operation.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. A commission can be a live, browser-based work with a fully named production record

The work page for Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley's [*I DIDNT REALISE YOU THOUGHT
LIKE THAT*](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/i-didnt-realise-you-thought-like-that/)
dates the project from 21 May 2026 onward and specifies web and mobile access
with subtitles. It describes a game built from the fictional world of *Below
the Blue Line*: negative online comments become events in a post-apocalyptic
world, and a real-time feed presents factions and competing accounts of truth.
The player decides whom or what to let through a door; those choices produce
different viewpoints and endings. The page names Serpentine Arts Technologies
as commissioner and producer, Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley as lead artist and
concept creator, Beyond Code Collective as a collaborator, Fonz Morris as
developer, and the curatorial and production team.

The public record demonstrates network-native commissioning through the work's
medium, access surfaces, interaction, credits, and current status. Preservation
status is not stated.

### 2. FAE3 turns infrastructure research into a dated, downloadable artifact

The [FAE3 launch page](https://www.serpentinegalleries.org/whats-on/future-art-ecosystems-3-live-art-x-decentralised-tech-launch/)
dates the online release to 25 November 2022 and calls FAE3 an annual
strategic briefing. It describes interviews with specialists in art,
decentralised technology, innovation policy, and civic practice; prospective
strategies for existing and new cultural organizations; and a participatory
Pol.is workshop asking how to build a more interoperable cultural sector.

The exact report, [*Future Art Ecosystems: Art x Decentralised Tech
(FAE3)*](https://futureartecosystems.org/briefing/fae3/), is a co-written and
edited publication with named contributors, advisors, researchers, designers,
and an associated artwork. Its opening pages place the report after the
decentralised-technology hype cycle and set out a “long(er) view” of cultural
infrastructure. The report maps legacy institutional systems against
decentralised proposals, then develops its argument through interviews and
operational questions. The result is public research with a method and an
edition. Its prospective strategies remain recommendations; adoption requires
separate evidence.

### 3. Legal inquiry is attached to concrete production and transaction problems

The Legal Lab's exact paper, [*The Legal Ambiguities of Art Collaborations and
their Compatibility with NFTs*](https://d37zoqglehb9o7.cloudfront.net/uploads/2020/05/Serpentine-Legal-Lab-Paper_Art-Collaborations-NFTs-FINAL-copy.pdf),
is by Alana Kushnir and dated 27 May 2021. It examines how NFT-platform terms
handle collaborative authorship during minting, sale, and resale. The paper
tests the problem against platform terms, distinguishes a singular-author
assumption from the actual labor of artists and technologists, and follows the
consequences through payment distribution, resale royalties, moral rights, and
crediting. It ends by asking collaborators to establish rights expectations and
platforms to make their terms more compatible with collaborative practice; it
also states that the paper is not legal advice.

The practice translates a production problem into a public document that identifies the
relevant terms, affected collaborators, unresolved ambiguity, and possible
design response.

### 4. One inquiry is published through several public surfaces

Serpentine's materials give an inquiry different forms without treating them
as interchangeable. *I DIDNT REALISE YOU THOUGHT LIKE THAT* is a playable web
and mobile commission with an access statement and production credits. FAE3
has a launch event, a downloadable report, a public workshop, and a separate
artifact site. Legal Lab has a programme page and a direct PDF research paper.
Together these surfaces give the work, research argument, event, and credit
record their own public routes.

## Close reading of public scholarship

The *I DIDNT REALISE YOU THOUGHT LIKE THAT* page begins with what the player
does and what the system does in response. Its writing moves from premise to
mechanic: the graphic-novel world, the simulated feed, the factions, the door,
and the consequences of choosing who enters. The page then shifts into a
production register that names the commission, producer, curator, artist,
developer, and collaborator. That sequence keeps the work legible before it
explains the institution around it. It also avoids a generic claim that
technology “changes society”; it identifies a feed, a gate, a choice, and a
different ending. The limitation is material and consequential: the page
documents a live online work as ongoing, not a preservation test or a stable
historical snapshot.

The Legal Lab paper uses a more formal research voice. Its headings follow the
transactional sequence—collaborative authorship and minting, first sale,
resale, royalties, conditions of sale, moral rights, and crediting. It moves
between the wording of platform terms and the practical situation of a
collaborating artist and technologist. It shows how a sole-author warranty,
automated payment rule, or broad platform licence
fails to describe the work's actual production. Its date matters: the reviewed
terms and platform list belong to May 2021, and its legal analysis cannot be
treated as current legal advice without jurisdiction-specific review.

FAE3 uses a different register again: a named, co-authored briefing that
combines systems diagrams, interviews, vocabulary, historical framing, and
prospective recommendations. Its writing openly moves between diagnosis and
speculation. That makes the document useful as an institutional-thinking
artifact, but it also marks the boundary between a published ambition and a
demonstrated operational change.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Commission network-native works with records that name the artist, developer, curator, producer, collaborators, access surface, device constraints, current status, and external dependencies.
- Publish infrastructure research as a dated artifact with named authors, contributors, method, source terms, and a clear label for recommendations that have not become policy.
- Make collaborative authorship and rights part of the acquisition and commissioning record: identify contributors, permissions, display and distribution rights, credit expectations, resale or revenue rules, and the governing jurisdiction.
- Give each inquiry the public form it needs: playable work, concise access record, longer essay or report, event documentation, downloadable artifact, and machine-readable identity where applicable.
- For chain-native works, test one exact commission through the whole lifecycle—commission, contract, mint or deployment, access, transfer, attribution, rights change, and migration—before generalizing the model.

## Where the analogy ends

- Serpentine's cited pages demonstrate commissioning, research, legal inquiry, and strategy publication. They do not demonstrate an accession workflow, chain custody, condition reporting, or long-term preservation. Do not import a preservation claim into this profile.
- FAE3 explicitly formulates prospective strategies. Its discussion of public cultural infrastructure is an argument and a design horizon, not evidence that its proposed interoperability or governance arrangements exist in the Museum.
- A playable page marked “ongoing” proves a current access route at the research date. It does not prove fixity, reproducibility across devices, source-code retention, dependency control, or future access.
- The Legal Lab paper's platform terms, examples, and legal analysis are dated 2021 and jurisdiction-sensitive. They are research inputs for a rights review, not a substitute for legal advice or an adopted Museum policy.
- A commission-led R&D programme has different obligations from a permanent collection. A chain-native museum must add title, custody, rights, preservation, correction, and accession gates after the experimental phase.

# San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.1
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

SFMOMA’s [Media Arts](https://www.sfmoma.org/artists-artworks/media-arts/)
page states that its Media Arts department was established in 1987. The page
lists video, film, slide, sound, computer-based, online, and live-performance
works, and connects collection highlights to online artworks, publications, and
media-preservation research. Its collection record for [Harrell Fletcher and
Miranda July; Yuri Ono and web designer, *Learning to Love You More*,
2002–2009](https://www.sfmoma.org/artwork/2010.45.A-EEEEEEEE/) identifies the
work as digital media, a web project and archive, acquired in 2010, and not on
view at the time of the record.

## Questions asked at acquisition

Jill Sterrett’s [“Matters in Media
Art”](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/matters-in-media-art/) describes media
artworks as dormant in storage and activated by viewers in the gallery. The
essay records SFMOMA’s need to ask artists about elaborate installation
setups, specialized technology, viewing conditions, and care appropriate to
the work’s intentions.

The same essay identifies the 1996 Team Media group as initially “a registrar,
a media tech, and me,” in Sterrett’s account. SFMOMA’s [“Team Media: In Action,
in Contemplation”](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/team-media-action-contemplation/)
describes its monthly meeting as bringing together curators, conservators,
technicians, intellectual-property managers, registrars, and web and digital
staff. It says the group began with three members and regularly attracts more
than fifteen interested people.

SFMOMA presents [“Matters in Media Art”](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/matters-in-media-art/) as an international collaboration among
the New Art Trust, The Museum of Modern Art, SFMOMA, and Tate. The essay says
the collaboration produced procedures and downloadable forms for lending
video, film, audio, and computer-based installations, and that practices are
adopted and revised as technology changes.

For the 6529 Network Museum, the accession gate for an executable work should
require a completed technical questionnaire with: artist installation
instructions; hardware, software, and service dependencies; significant
properties; active and dormant test results; named change authority; artist or
estate contacts; rights to preserve source and dependencies; and an approved
fallback manifestation. A cross-functional review should sign the record
before accession, and each later revision should cite the case that prompted
it.

## Writing from practice

SFMOMA publishes two complementary editorial forms. The [*Learning to Love You
More* collection record](https://www.sfmoma.org/artwork/2010.45.A-EEEEEEEE/)
combines a concise object description with classification, medium, dates,
acquisition, credit, copyright, permanent URL, and display status. Sterrett’s
longer [“Matters in Media Art”](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/matters-in-media-art/)
names the staff group, the acquisition questions, the partner institutions,
and the downloadable forms. Together, the pages connect a stable object
record to the institutional reasoning around its care.

The Museum should use the same editorial division: keep facts and status in
the object record, and publish the technical decisions, participants,
uncertainties, and revision history in linked practitioner essays.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Add the technical questionnaire and cross-functional approval to the
  accession checklist for every executable or service-dependent work.
- Store separate dormant and activated condition observations, each with date,
  environment, test result, and evidence link.
- Assign a named authority for hardware substitution, software migration,
  dependency replacement, and fallback display.
- Publish reusable forms with version numbers, adoption dates, and amendment
  notes tied to specific casework.
- Create a standing media review that includes curation, conservation,
  registration, technical operations, rights, and web or digital staff.

## Where the analogy ends

SFMOMA’s Team Media account presupposes a staffed museum with registrars,
conservators, technicians, rights staff, and digital staff who can meet
regularly. The Museum must name equivalent roles, fund outside
partners where needed, and record responsibility in each object file. The
downloadable form does not settle artist-specific rights or significant
properties; those remain work-level decisions.

## Sources

1. SFMOMA, [“Media Arts”](https://www.sfmoma.org/artists-artworks/media-arts/).
2. SFMOMA, [“Harrell Fletcher and Miranda July; Yuri Ono and web designer Learning to Love You More, 2002-2009”](https://www.sfmoma.org/artwork/2010.45.A-EEEEEEEE/).
3. Jill Sterrett, [“Matters in Media Art”](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/matters-in-media-art/), SFMOMA, October 2015.
4. Lindsey Westbrook, [“Team Media: In Action, in Contemplation”](https://www.sfmoma.org/read/team-media-action-contemplation/), SFMOMA, February 2016.

# Tate

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.1
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

Tate's Net Art Commissions record makes archival loss and reconstruction part of
the public record. The [Tate Public Records catalogue](https://archive.tate.org.uk/Record.aspx?id=TG+100%2F1&src=CalmView.Catalog)
says that most of the original records were accidentally lost between 2016 and
2018. It separates recovered original material, reconstituted records, and an
archived version of the Intermedia Art microsite. It also names the recovery
sources and states that a cataloguer created an artificial order because the
original order could not be followed. The catalogue record itself demonstrates
the archival practice.

## Close reading: Net Art Commissions and the Intermedia Art Microsite

The [series record](https://archive.tate.org.uk/Record.aspx?id=TG+100%2F1&src=CalmView.Catalog)
identifies fifteen internet and software-based artworks commissioned between
2000 and 2012. The [Intermedia Art Microsite record](https://archive.tate.org.uk/Record.aspx?id=TG+100%2F1%2F9&src=CalmView.Catalog)
describes the 2008–2012 microsite that gathered those works with contextual
texts, interviews, events, broadcasts, and podcasts.

Its conservation description is unusually exact. Tate records a Conifer capture
made between November 2019 and February 2020, explains that the capture was
organized by artwork and other site sections, says that only the first page of
external links was captured, and records the merging of section-level WARC
files. It also names the failures: three works were unavailable because their
artists no longer hosted them; *Uncomfortable Proximity* could not be
experienced in full; and the podcasts were not archived. The record therefore
describes a bounded access manifestation and states its omissions.

For the 6529 Network Museum, a reconstructed record should expose the same
distinctions:

- record whether each assertion is original, recovered, reconstituted, or
  derived from a later capture;
- publish the source inventory, reconstruction method, artificial order,
  author, date, confidence, and superseded record;
- state capture date, scope, external-link policy, package/fixity reference,
  runtime or emulation conditions, unavailable components, and current access
  status;
- keep token identity, metadata, dependencies, platform behavior, community
  context, and exhibition history as separate assertions.

## Research and conservation: Reshaping the Collectible

The archive identifies [Reshaping the Collectible: The Lives of Net Art](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/reshaping-the-collectible#the-lives-of-net-art)
as the 2021 Tate Research Publication that supplied the research context for
reconstituting the lost records. It also names Lucy Bayley's
[“Net Art: Dusty Navigational Pathways”](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/reshaping-the-collectible/net-art-dusty-navigational-pathways)
as a chapter in that publication. The archive further records that Tate's
Public Records and Time-Based Media Conservation teams worked together on the
microsite and reconstitution process.

The writing's strength is procedural: it identifies what was found, what was
reconstructed, how the order was made, and what remains unavailable. That
method gives a chain-native museum a usable scholarly form for uncertainty.
Disclosure of recovery and intervention is the practice to adopt. The record
treats web capture as a partial manifestation with documented boundaries.

## What the Museum should adopt

- publish reconstruction lineage as part of the record, not as an invisible
  editorial process;
- bind every public technical claim to a dated capture, source package, or
  observation;
- record the authority and rationale for consequential changes to metadata,
  dependencies, runtime, or display behavior;
- expose incomplete access and unresolved components beside the public
  manifestation;
- issue a new, attributable record when a later reconstruction supersedes an
  earlier one.

## Where the analogy ends

Tate's evidence concerns a historical public-records workflow and a specific
2018–2022 research project. It does not show that every networked artwork can
be recovered, that every capture is complete, or that the historical capture
tool remains available. The Museum should adopt the explicit boundaries and
lineage, then test its own preservation packages against its own works and
dependencies.

2. Tate Archive, [“Intermedia Art Microsite”](https://archive.tate.org.uk/Record.aspx?id=TG+100%2F1%2F9&src=CalmView.Catalog), 2008–2012 record date shown.
3. Tate, [“Reshaping the Collectible: The Lives of Net Art”](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/reshaping-the-collectible#the-lives-of-net-art), 2021.
4. Lucy Bayley, [“Net Art: Dusty Navigational Pathways”](https://www.tate.org.uk/research/reshaping-the-collectible/net-art-dusty-navigational-pathways), 2021.

# transmediale

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

## Institutional profile

The 2012 conference *transmediale Unarchived* made the archive itself a
program subject. Its public account brings together a 25-year institutional
history, archive digitization, online dissemination, and the question of how
curators can return archival material to interpretation and circulation.
[transmediale Unarchived](https://archive.transmediale.de/content/transmediale-unarchived)

This is a useful starting point for the Museum because transmediale's archive
and program are interdependent. The archive records how a festival and its
publication forms changed as internet art, software art, online programs, and
hybrid events changed around it.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. A long program history is made browseable by edition

The legacy archive presents annual festival history from 1988 through 2020 in
a year-and-edition structure, with special projects and related material. The
organization describes transmediale e.V. as an independent nonprofit that
maintains documentation and archives, produces print and online publications,
and runs residencies and commissions. [Archive overview](https://archive.transmediale.de/archive)
· [Organization](https://transmediale.de/de/organisation)

### 2. Publication is a continuing institutional record

The journal is an online platform for essays, conversations, and interviews,
with issue and publication-type filters. It supplies a scholarly layer around
the program, beyond event metadata. [Journal](https://archive.transmediale.de/journal/articles)

The 2016 *Across and Beyond* publication provides a second form: an edited
introduction to post-digital practices, concepts, and institutions. Its
editorial apparatus lets institutional interpretation travel with the project.
[Across and Beyond](https://archive.transmediale.de/content/across-and-beyond-post-digital-practices-concepts-and-institutions)

### 3. Program formats and original files remain part of the history

The current history records the 2021–2022 *for refusal* program, including an
Almanac updated monthly at the full moon and a microcomputer-based ceramic
portal with original files. The record therefore links event duration, online
publication, technical format, and retained source material. [History](https://transmediale.de/en/history)

## Close reading of public scholarship

transmediale's writing changes register with its subject. The archive overview
is chronological and navigational; *Unarchived* is reflective and asks what
archival work does; the journal is issue-based and discursive; the current
history tracks shifts in medium and event format. Together these forms produce
institutional memory without pretending that every program item has the same
status or completeness.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Give festivals, commissions, publications, online programs, residencies,
  archives, and artworks separate records with typed relationships.
- Preserve edition, date, format, original files, migration history, current
  access route, and later interpretation for every significant program.
- Treat publications as durable research objects with authors, contributors,
  issue/date, source files, revision history, and suggested citation.
- Keep an archive's historical cutoff, missing material, reconstructed pages,
  and current access defects visible.
- Record program material that is temporarily online as a lifecycle state with
  an explicit preservation status.

## Where the analogy ends

transmediale's archive is festival history and public scholarship. The reviewed
material does not establish title, accession, custody, condition, or
object-level conservation. The apparent 2020 endpoint of the legacy archive
and the absence of a public structured API should remain explicit. The record
should carry those gaps without inference.

# Victoria and Albert Museum

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.1
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The V&A’s public conservation writing documents a digital-care program being
built through casework, equipment, workflows, and collaboration. Anna
Mladentseva’s [“What does conserving the digital look
like?”](https://www.vam.ac.uk/blog/projects/what-does-conserving-the-digital-look-like)
describes the museum’s first dedicated digital conservation studio and the
work required to establish disk imaging, write-blocking, and related
procedures.

## *Shaping Form 14/5/2007*: a documented intervention

Mladentseva describes Ernest Edmonds’s *Shaping Form 14/5/2007* as a MacMini
connected to a liquid-crystal display monitor, with a USB camera embedded in
the monitor frame. The software, programmed primarily in Max/MSP, responds to
movement by generating vertical bands of varying thickness and colour.

For this work, the article reports that the conservator disassembled the
artist-provided MacMini, changed an internal battery, extracted the hard drive,
and made a bit-for-bit disk image with a forensic imager and write-blocker.
The image preserves file and directory structures, the operating system, and
deleted files, and can support later migration or emulation. Legacy adapters
were required to read the drive, and dust removal was completed during
reassembly.

The work was then run with original artist-provided parts and assessed in both
dormant and activated states. The conservator recorded Max/MSP console errors
and assessed whether they affected the work. The article reports treatment
proposals and a preservation plan, analysis of Max/MSP, Jitter, and Java source
code, and recovery of multiple versions of software-architecture documents
from deleted files. It presents those materials as evidence for understanding
the program’s functionality, artistic intention, and making process.

The 6529 Network Museum should publish case studies with the same minimum
structure: object definition, environment, intervention trigger, tools and
risks, fixity evidence, condition observations, source and dependency findings,
artist or estate input, decision authority, and follow-up preservation plan.

## Collection access around real use

Kati Price’s [“Redesigning the V&A’s collections
online”](https://www.vam.ac.uk/blog/digital/redesigning-the-vas-collections-online)
states that V&A collections information was distributed across three public
locations and seven systems. It identifies object pages with no onward paths
as “digital culs-de-sac” and describes a redesign intended to connect objects
with makers, themes, stories, research, and making.

For 6529, an object page should expose links to the project, artist, chain and
provenance events, technical dependencies, related works, conservation builds,
and correction or amendment history. A catalogue review should test actual
questions: can a visitor move from token to artist and project; can a researcher
compare media, dependencies, or provenance events; and can a contributor locate
the governing source and propose a correction?

## What the Museum should adopt

- Record original environment, active and dormant condition, intervention
  trigger, tools, fixity results, errors, dependencies, source versions, and
  rights in every digital-work record.
- Require a preservation plan when an object depends on removable media,
  obsolete hardware, proprietary software, external services, or artist-made
  code.
- Link each intervention to an evidence package containing images, logs,
  version identifiers, treatment decisions, and artist or estate responses.
- Separate the stable object record from dated practitioner essays, then link
  both directions.
- Test collection navigation with visitor and research tasks before treating a
  catalogue redesign as complete.

## Where the analogy ends

The V&A’s *Shaping Form* account is one documented case, and the article says
source-code access depended on support from the artist. Its public writing also
describes digital-care workflows as newly established. The Museum should not
assume that source, hardware, or third-party service access will be
available; it should record those absences, rights limits, and unresolved
dependencies at accession.

## Sources

2. Katherine Mitchell, [“Why things fail and why it matters: some challenges for digital collecting today – Part 2”](https://www.vam.ac.uk/blog/digital/why-things-fail-and-why-it-matters-some-challenges-for-digital-collecting-today-part-2), V&A, 16 August 2023.
3. Kati Price, [“Redesigning the V&A’s collections online”](https://www.vam.ac.uk/blog/digital/redesigning-the-vas-collections-online), V&A, 30 May 2019.

- **Series:** A field of practice

## Institutional profile

V2_'s [About the Archive](https://v2.nl/articles/about-the-archive/) opens by
limiting its own authority. The archive documents V2_ history, includes only
material with a direct relation to V2_, and says that completeness and
correctness are not guaranteed. It invites additions and corrections through
the editorial team. The archive includes events, people, artworks, essays,
interviews, publications, old websites, video, audio, photographs, and a
library.

That scope statement is itself a preservation record. It tells a researcher
what the archive is trying to do, what it cannot promise, and how a later person
can challenge it.

## Demonstrated practices

### 1. Migration history is part of archive description

V2_ reports that online content was migrated from an older archive in 2010
after the old software created a security problem. It identifies a DVD/disk
image route and notes that some image and movie material was excluded. Its
rights statement gives CC BY-SA as a general position while preserving
author- and photographer-specific exceptions.

### 2. Unstable-media research produces reusable structures

The 2003 *Capturing Unstable Media* project used the case studies *whisper* and
*DataCloud 2.0* to address documentation and preservation of unstable media.
Its recommendations cover documentation strategy, formal modeling, metadata,
and archival interoperability. [Capturing Unstable Media](https://v2.nl/works/capturing-unstable-media/)

The proposed structure is valuable because it treats documentation as an
interoperability problem. A future archive should be able to understand the
work, its relations, and its preservation decisions without depending on one
interface.

### 3. The archive is distributed across institutional relationships

V2_'s account of the Network for the Archiving of Design and Digital Culture,
launched 17 December 2020, describes a model that is centralized where needed
and decentralized where possible. Access, usability, resilience, and a network
of archives are treated as related design concerns. [V2_ part of Network for
the Archiving of Design and Digital Culture](https://v2.nl/blog/v2_-part-of-network-for-the-archiving-of-design-and-digital-culture)

The current catalogue supplies a public discovery surface, while V2_'s
reflection on forty years of archiving describes lost or destroyed material and
the archive as a continuing construction. [Catalogue](https://v2.nl/search/all/catalogue)
· [About 40 years of Archiving Unstable Media Art](https://v2.nl/articles/about-40-years-of-archiving-unstable-media-art/)

## Close reading of public scholarship

V2_ writes about archives through declared incompleteness. The archive page is
an editorial policy; *Capturing Unstable Media* is a research report with
methods and recommendations; the forty-year reflection is a conversation about
loss, selection, and construction. The community survey of iconic works is
useful as program and archival input, but its voting result should not be
turned into a collection-significance metric.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Give every public archive a scope statement naming inclusion rule, exclusions,
  date range, authority, correction route, and current completeness.
- Record migration trigger, old software, retained disk image or export,
  excluded material, new route, license, and known access defects.
- Use stable Museum identifiers and typed relationships among works, events,
  artists, publications, people, captures, and preservation actions.
- Publish correction and supersession paths so the archive can become more
  accurate without erasing its earlier state.
- Treat distributed storage and partner archives as named custody/access
  relationships with named custody and access roles.

## Where the analogy ends

V2_'s archive is program history and institutional memory. It does not establish
title, custody, accession, condition, or conservation completion. The current
[archive route](https://v2.nl/archive) returned HTTP 200 in a focused check but
rendered the site's page-not-found state in browser inspection on 2026-08-04;
that content-level access defect belongs in the record alongside the working
article and catalogue routes.

# Walker Art Center

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

Walker Art Center's interdisciplinary collecting practice treats a live work as
a chain of commission, presentation, documentation, acquisition, training, and
future presentation. The [Interdisciplinary Initiative](https://www.walkerart.org/interdisciplinary-initiative/)
describes this chain through named projects. Maria Hassabi's *STAGING: solo*
was acquired in collaboration with the artist with a training plan, while the
page distinguishes archival and sculptural iterations from the live work. Jason
Moran's multipart project links commission, exhibition, catalogue, concerts,
digital publication, acquisition, and future stage guidelines.

## Collecting performance without collapsing ownership and documentation

Susannah Schouweiler's ["Collecting Performance"](https://www.walkerart.org/reader/collecting-performance/)
(December 15, 2011) records a Walker workshop involving scholars, writers,
developers, performers, presenters, archivists, curators, and videographers.
Its questions are concrete: what is collected and tagged; who controls
documentation; how do ownership, authorship, and profit-sharing differ; and how
can an archive make the traces of performance encounterable to a public.

The essay reports a distinction that matters for 6529: a commissioning or
collecting institution may hold documentation or a public commitment without
owning the artist's entire performance practice. Walker's language of a
"living archive" describes traces, recordings, notes, scores, rehearsals,
sets, costumes, and audience responses as related evidence, not as identical
substitutes for the event.

The [Walker Collection](https://www.walkerart.org/art-artists/visual-arts/walker-collection/)
page adds an acquisition sequence: strategic planning, board approval,
accession, and an artist questionnaire issued by registrars. It describes a
Long-Range Acquisitions Plan developed through extended institutional dialogue.
The page demonstrates a process claim; it does not establish that every public
object page exposes the full process.

## Living Collections Catalogue and publication genre

Walker publishes interdisciplinary research through essays, commissions,
videos, and the [Living Collections Catalogue](https://www.walkerart.org/interdisciplinary-initiative/).
The writing is project-sequential: it identifies the commission, the public
presentation, the acquired manifestation, the training or documentation needed
to repeat it, and the future conditions under which it may be shown. Walker's
[publishing page](https://www.walkerart.org/walker-publishing/print-publications/)
also makes editors, designers, contributors, object entries, essays, and artist
collaboration visible as part of the publication record.

For the 6529 Network Museum, a live or performative work should have a
manifestation ledger with separate entries for commission, event, installation,
archive, acquired rights, artist instructions, training, and future guidelines.
The Museum should record ownership, documentation rights, display authority,
and acceptable change as different assertions. An artist questionnaire should
be versioned, attributed, and linked to the accession or commission it informs.

## What the Museum should adopt

- Model live works as linked manifestations. A stable work record connects the
  events without flattening them into one object state.
- Preserve the distinction between ownership, documentation, archive, and
  public presentation.
- Record artist instructions, training, future-stage guidance, and the authority
  for changes to each manifestation.
- Link commission, exhibition, publication, acquisition, and archive events by
  date and stable identifier.
- Credit editors, designers, artists, researchers, and technical contributors
  in the publication record.

## Where the analogy ends

Walker’s strongest evidence concerns performance, interdisciplinary commissions,
and an institutional discussion published in 2011. The model depends on
performance-specific labor, artist relationships, board process, and a large
library and archive. It is not public evidence of a general digital-conservation
workflow. The Museum should transfer the manifestation and authority model,
not claim equivalent staffing or preservation capacity.

# Whitney Museum of American Art

- **Series:** A field of practice
- **Status:** public scholarship
- **Institutional author:** 6529 Network Museum
- **Version:** 1.0.0
- **Publication date:** 2026-08-04
- **Research cutoff:** 2026-08-04
- **Research apparatus:** [primary-source register](../source-register.md)

The Whitney's collection and digital-art programs connect collection records,
online commissions, conservation, and artist documentation. Its collection
page reports more than 27,000 works by more than 4,100 artists and provides
filters for digital art, film, video, installation, sound, and artport. These
filters are discovery tools with changing counts. Treat their results as
time-specific interface states; keep fixed inventory totals in governed records.
([Collection](https://whitney.org/collection/works))

The resulting architecture supports different encounters. A browser-based work
requires an address and an account of its dependencies. A moving-image work
requires duration and playback conditions. A restored commission requires a
record of the intervention and the historical state that preceded it.

## Douglas Davis: one work, several public states

The Whitney's public account of Douglas Davis's *The World's First Collaborative
Sentence* identifies the work as launched in 1994 and restored in 2013. It
records the 1995 acquisition, donor, commission, programmers, media formats,
and artist statement. The page presents a live version and a restored historic
version as distinct manifestations. ([Douglas Davis, *The World's First Collaborative Sentence*](https://whitney.org/artport/douglas-davis))

The conservation account names concrete failures: a CGI script was omitted
during server migration, malformed user contributions affected display, visitor
links decayed, and Korean characters remained partly illegible after the
character set was addressed. The live version accepts contributions and links
to a GitHub route for further work on the Korean text. The historic version
keeps its code largely untouched, disallows contributions, and preserves known
legibility defects. ([Douglas Davis, *The World's First Collaborative Sentence*](https://whitney.org/artport/douglas-davis))

This gives the 6529 Network Museum a concrete manifestation model. A live
generator, historical deployment, emulation, conservation build, and still
capture should each have a typed status, date, source, and relation to the
accessioned work. A public repair route should create a reviewed proposal or
technical record. It should not silently change the canonical work record.

## artport as program and archive

The Whitney describes artport as an online portal launched in 2001 for internet
art, commissions, exhibitions, resources, and collection presentations. Its
historical architecture separates commissions, exhibitions, resources, and a
collection area for networked and digital works. ([artport](https://whitney.org/artport/); [artport historical architecture](https://artport.whitney.org/v2/about.shtml))

The program establishes a useful publication rule: a live commission, its
documentation, and its archived version require different records. A current
commission should carry its dates, artist, technical dependencies, and access
conditions. A historical record should preserve the earlier address, capture,
intervention history, and known failures. The existence of a page alone does
not establish preservation of the work's prior behavior.

## Conservation and artist documentation

The Whitney's Conservation department reports a time-based-media program
covering film, video, audio, 35mm slide, and digital art. Its Artists
Documentation Program records conversations between artists and conservators
about materials, process, intent, and change. The department also describes a
Replication Committee whose participants include conservation, curatorial,
registration, collection management, legal, rights, and publication roles.
([Conservation](https://whitney.org/conservation))

The Media Preservation Initiative reports work across approximately 800
collection works. It developed cataloguing standards, rehoused physical media,
conducted historical and technical research, and built a digital-preservation
pipeline. Its public materials include acquisition questionnaires, media
reports, installation information, and condition reports. The re-cataloguing
of Nam June Paik's *Magnet TV* is a concrete example: components were
photographed and relabelled, and the catalogue was checked against current
standards. ([Media Preservation Initiative](https://whitney.org/conservation/mpi))

For the 6529 Network Museum, accession diligence should record artist or
representative interviews, significant properties, runtime and dependency
information, installation authority, rights, condition, preservation action,
and the reason for any replication or migration decision. The record should
identify whether a statement is artist voice, technical observation, or Museum
interpretation.

## Collection publishing and public data

Whitney's Open Access page describes nightly CSV exports containing much of the
artist and artwork information published online. Its API documentation provides
REST JSON access to artists, artworks, exhibitions, events, guides, and pages;
it recommends TMS artwork identifiers as canonical identifiers because they are
less likely to change than internal IDs. The documentation also warns that
fields may change and that older, pre-internet records are less complete. It
provides usage, citation, and contact guidance. ([Open Access](https://whitney.org/open-access); [API](https://whitney.org/about/website/api))

The operational lesson is to publish a canonical Museum identifier beside
chain identifiers, record the source system and observation date, document API
stability, and state where historical records are incomplete. Public exports
should carry rights and attribution instructions. An API should be treated as
a delivery layer over versioned records, with a migration path when fields or
source systems change.

## Public scholarship and writing method

The Douglas Davis page places object identity, interpretation, artist statement,
acquisition and donor history, technical failures, conservation credits,
installation documentation, live and historic versions, and contribution links
within one navigable account. Its writing moves from the work's participatory
form to specific failures and then to the consequences of preservation choices.

The Whitney's conservation pages use a procedural register: they identify the
media surveyed, standards created, physical actions taken, technical research,
and documentation templates. Together, the sampled pages show how a public
record can remain readable while exposing the evidence needed for a researcher,
conservator, or contributor.

## What the Museum should adopt

The 6529 Network Museum should publish each accession through connected layers:

- a concise object record with stable identity, accession, credit, rights, and
  status;
- a work page with close looking and interpretation;
- manifestation records for live, historical, restored, and documentary states;
- technical, condition, preservation, and artist-documentation records;
- a machine-readable export and a reviewed correction route.

## Where the analogy ends

The Whitney's artport projects and Douglas Davis restoration are specific
program histories. They do not establish that every digital work in the
collection has equivalent preservation depth. The collection interface and API
are dynamic, and the API documentation itself identifies field changes and
uneven completeness across historical records.

The 6529 Network Museum should adopt the manifestation, defect, contribution,
and identifier practices. It should retain institutional selection and review
for accession, treat public submissions as evidence requiring evaluation, and
preserve historical states even when a live version has been repaired.

ZKM was founded in 1989 by the City of Karlsruhe and the state of
Baden-Württemberg. Its planning began in 1984 and took formal shape in
“Konzept ’88.” The founding model joined a museum and media-art collection
with research institutes, studios, and a media theatre; ZKM’s current

performances, collections, and archives. [Founding & History](https://zkm.de/en/founding-history) · [Development & Philosophy](https://zkm.de/en/development-philosophy)

ZKM reports approximately 12,000 works, 24,000 video and audio tapes, more

of more than 9,000 titles. These are current institutional figures, not
independent measurements. [The ZKM Collection](https://zkm.de/en/the-zkm-collection)

## Work record: *Wipe Cycle*

The official record for Frank Gillette and Ira Schneider’s *Wipe Cycle* keeps
the 1969 work, its later reconstruction, and its technical dependencies in
one public account. The record identifies a six-channel installation with
nine cathode-ray monitors, a camera, two digitized analog videos, six
Raspberry Pi 3B+ computers, Raspian, custom C/GStreamer software, a custom
video-switch board, sound, a media player, and speakers. It also links an
installation view and the 1969 schematic. [Wipe Cycle](https://zkm.de/de/werk/wipe-cycle)

The apparatus explains the work’s closed-circuit timing, so the equipment list
remains attached to the work's operation.
The record distinguishes historical documentation from the reconstruction,
but it contains a dating issue: the narrative places the reconstruction in a
2017 exhibition while image captions show both 1969/2017 and 1969/2018. That
uncertainty should remain visible until the source institution resolves it.

For the 6529 Network Museum, every migration or emulation record should retain
the original runtime, current runtime, preserved source, intervention date,
decision-maker, evidence links, and known differences between states.

## Conservation and research as operating infrastructure

ZKM describes a restoration team combining restoration, electrical engineering,
computer science, and art history. The team documents and restores works while
developing standardized documentation and long-term conservation methods.
[Restoration of Electronic and Digital Art](https://zkm.de/en/restoration-of-electronic-and-digital-art)

Its Laboratory for Antiquated Video Systems was founded in 2004. ZKM reports
that the laboratory maintains more than 300 historical video devices and can
digitize nearly fifty formats; it also describes metadata, mirroring, and the
continued value of analog holdings alongside digital copies. [Laboratory for Antiquated Video Systems](https://zkm.de/en/laboratory-for-antiquated-video-systems)

In 2017, ZKM created “Wissen – Collection, Archives & Research,” bringing
together collection fields with the institutional archive and acquired archives
of artists and theorists. [Wissen](https://zkm.de/en/wissen) ZKM also published
the 665-page *Digital Art Conservation* anthology in 2013, presenting results
of a project begun in 2010 through case studies and contributions from
theorists, restorers, programmers, and artists. [Digital Art Conservation](https://zkm.de/en/publications/digital-art-conservation)

## What the Museum should adopt

- Require a technical-constitution record for executable or networked works:
  source, dependencies, runtime, media inputs, display behavior, and capture
  conditions.
- Record original, migrated, emulated, and exhibited states separately, with
  dates, responsible reviewers, evidence, and known losses or changes.
- Route review to the competencies the work requires—art history, code or
  contract behavior, rights, infrastructure, and conservation—and retain the
  review roles with the object record.
- Publish a concise public record alongside the technical note, preservation
  history, and sources that allow another researcher to reproduce the claim.

## Where the analogy ends

ZKM’s laboratories, obsolete-equipment holdings, physical facilities, and
public funding support a material preservation program that the 6529 Network
Museum cannot reproduce at equivalent scale online. ZKM’s claims about global
size or uniqueness remain institutional self-report; the transferable evidence
is the documented record structure, conservation workflow, and explicit
handling of reconstruction states.

# Rights in digital art

Copyright shapes how an artwork can be shown, studied, preserved, circulated,
and transformed. Artists, collectors, and museums hold different
responsibilities for those uses. A public license can make the terms legible in
advance. This handbook explains the rights language the 6529 Network Museum is
likely to encounter and how each term bears on museum work and public reuse.

## Copyright in brief

Copyright generally begins when an original work is fixed in a form from which
it can be perceived or reproduced. Berne Convention countries protect works
without requiring registration or another formality. National law determines
the details, duration, exceptions, and remedies.

Copyright commonly gives its owner control over reproduction, distribution,
public display or performance, and the preparation of adaptations. These
rights can be licensed separately. Some countries also recognize moral rights,
including an artist's claim to authorship and protection against prejudicial
alteration.

Ideas, systems, procedures, and methods are distinct from the particular
expression that copyright protects. A generative artwork may contain several
protected layers: source code, visual output, sound, text, typefaces, a user
interface, documentation, and third-party libraries or assets. One rights
label should be applied only to the components it actually covers.

## Two useful starting points

### Buying the artwork usually does not buy its copyright

A collector can own an object while the artist owns copyright in the work it
embodies. Museums have worked with that division for generations: a museum may
own a painting while the artist or the artist's estate controls reproduction
rights. Digital art follows the same basic pattern. The token, the work, and
copyright are separate interests unless an agreement joins them.

A collector may own the token, its place in an edition, and the associated
files or records, subject to the governing terms. Copyright ownership answers
who controls certain uses of the artistic expression.

### The public domain is where much of art history lives

The public domain is neither an exceptional nor a suspect condition. Copyright
lasts for a limited term. When that term ends, the work becomes available for
people to reproduce, study, publish, reinterpret, and place in new works.

Leonardo's *Mona Lisa*, Vermeer's *Girl with a Pearl Earring*, Hokusai's *Under
the Wave off Kanagawa*, and Van Gogh's *The Starry Night* are familiar examples
of works whose copyrights have expired. Their presence in books, classrooms,
films, scholarship, posters, and digital archives shows what the public domain
does: it keeps cultural inheritance available for new attention.

A particular photograph, scan, edition, or website may raise a separate rights
or contract question. The status of that file should not be confused with the
status of the underlying artwork. The Public Domain Mark helps institutions
communicate a reviewed worldwide public-domain determination. CC0 lets a
rights holder place a newer work as fully as possible into that field of free
use.

## The token and the work

An NFT identifies a token on a blockchain. It may point to media or help prove
the history of a transaction. Copyright in the associated artwork remains a
separate legal interest. A token sale transfers copyright only when an
effective agreement says so.

That distinction has practical consequences. A collector may own the token
while the artist retains copyright. The artist may give every holder a public
license, grant narrower holder rights, or make no additional grant. Platform
terms may supply another part of the answer. The controlling evidence should
travel with the work: the exact license text, its version, the metadata in
which it appeared, the relevant platform terms, and any signed agreement.

The 2024 joint study by the United States Copyright Office and Patent and
Trademark Office identified public education and product transparency as
central responses to confusion about NFTs and intellectual property. This
handbook treats clear rights information as part of the work's public record.

## Four questions to ask

### Who owns the relevant right?

The artist is often the first copyright owner, although employment,
commissioning terms, collaboration, and earlier transfers can change that
answer. A licensor can grant only rights that the licensor holds or is
authorized to grant.

### What exactly is covered?

The answer may be the rendered image, the live program, the source code, the
sound, the text, or some combination. Dependencies and contributed elements
may have their own licenses. The Museum records components separately when
their terms differ.

### What permission applies?

A Creative Commons license supplies public permission under stated
conditions. CC0 is a dedication and fallback license. The Public Domain Mark
reports a status. RightsStatements.org terms help cultural institutions report
copyright and reuse status; they are not licenses. A custom agreement must be
read on its own terms. Silence supplies no public license to the world. It does
not prevent the lawful owner of a work from collecting, displaying,
documenting, studying, and caring for it in the ordinary course of museum
practice.

### What else remains?

Copyright is one part of the picture. Trademark, patent, privacy, publicity,
moral rights, contract, cultural-heritage law, and rules concerning personal
data may still matter. A license may also leave uses permitted by copyright
exceptions untouched.

## Reading the Creative Commons family

Creative Commons offers six current 4.0 International licenses. Their names
state the conditions:

- **BY: Attribution.** Credit the creator, retain supplied notices, link to
  the license, and identify changes.
- **SA: ShareAlike.** A shared adaptation must use the same or a compatible
  license.
- **NC: NonCommercial.** The licensed use must not be primarily directed
  toward commercial advantage or monetary compensation. The user's nonprofit
  status does not settle the character of the use.
- **ND: NoDerivatives.** Unadapted material may be shared. Adapted material
  may be made privately, but the license does not permit it to be shared.

The six combinations are CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA,
and CC BY-NC-ND. The 4.0 licenses permit technical changes needed to exercise
their licensed rights. They also prohibit downstream legal or technical
restrictions that would prevent another person from using the licensed
material on the same terms.

Creative Commons licenses are designed to endure. Once applied by an
authorized rights holder, a 4.0 license cannot be revoked for people who
continue to comply. An artist may stop distributing new copies under that
license or offer different terms in parallel, while existing licensed copies
retain the original grant.

Older, ported, or jurisdiction-specific Creative Commons licenses are separate
legal instruments. The Museum records the exact version and jurisdiction. It
does not silently translate an older license into 4.0.

## CC0 and the Public Domain Mark

**CC0 1.0** lets a rights holder waive copyright and related rights as fully as
the law permits. It includes a broad fallback license where a waiver cannot
take effect. CC0 does not require attribution, although museums should still
credit the artist and describe changes as a matter of scholarship.

**Public Domain Mark 1.0** is used for a work believed to be free of known
copyright restrictions worldwide. It does not waive rights or grant a
license. The mark follows a copyright determination; it does not create one.

## When no public license is stated

The Museum treats a protected work with no identified public license as an
in-copyright work. That classification concerns copyright ownership and public
reuse. The work remains available for collection display and study.

A lawfully acquired artwork belongs in the collection. Museums ordinarily
display such works, publish collection records with faithful identification
views, reproduce them where necessary for criticism and scholarship, and make
controlled copies needed for preservation. In the United States, ownership of
a lawfully made physical copy carries a statutory right to display that copy
to viewers present at its location. In the United Kingdom, public exhibition
of an artistic work is generally outside the acts restricted by copyright.
Online documentation, scholarship, and digital preservation draw on licenses,
agreements, fair use or fair dealing, statutory exceptions, and the
professional practices developed by museums for their public mission.

Digital and NFT works require the same separation of questions. The token does
not transfer copyright by itself. Yet a network-native work was made to be
seen through code, files, and public network references. Its acquisition,
artist instructions, mint terms, canonical presentation, and ordinary mode of
viewing form part of the Museum's basis for faithful display. The Museum
records those facts as evidence for presentation, scholarship, and care.

The closer review belongs at the edge of ordinary museum use. Public remixes,
merchandise, advertising, image licensing, endorsement, high-resolution
substitute files, and uses governed by a contrary artist, donor, lender, or
acquisition agreement each require their own basis. Faithful technical
migration for conservation is recorded as stewardship; a new artistic work is
treated as an adaptation.

## Rights statements used by cultural institutions

RightsStatements.org publishes twelve standardized labels for cultural
heritage collections. Five concern works in copyright, four concern works
outside copyright with remaining limits or a jurisdictional boundary, and
three describe unresolved status. They give visitors a concise status signal
and a stable URI. The detailed Museum rights record remains the place for the
underlying evidence, permissions, restrictions, and component-level detail.

These statements describe rights status and reuse conditions. “In Copyright”
assumes that the institution has a basis for making the item available.
“Copyright Not Evaluated” and “Copyright Undetermined” describe the state of
research. “No Known Copyright” records a reasoned conclusion without
presenting it as certainty. The Museum pairs each label with the evidence
supporting display, documentation, scholarship, preservation, and broader
reuse.

The rights registry in this repository contains all twelve statements and
links to their official definitions. A rights statement should appear close
to the object it describes.
